title: Hot Potato Debate
desc: Students pass a ball while music plays. When it stops, the holder must instantly give an argument.
steps: Play upbeat music while students pass a ball or object around the circle.
Stop the music randomly.
Display a controversial but lighthearted topic (e.g., 'Cats are better than dogs').
The student holding the object must immediately give one argument FOR or AGAINST.
Resume music immediately to keep energy high.
variation: Use 'Truth or Dare' questions instead of debate topics for a fun ice-breaker.
goal: Build spontaneous speaking fluency and persuasive reasoning under playful time pressure.
example: Board prompts: 'Cats vs. Dogs', 'Homework should be banned'. Sentence frame: 'I think ___ because ___.'

tips.lower_level: Write 2–3 opinion starters on the board ('In my opinion...', 'I agree/disagree because...') and allow 5 seconds of think time.
tips.higher_level: Require students to rebut the previous speaker's point before giving their own ('Even though Ana said..., I believe...').
tips.management: Use a soft foam ball or crumpled paper ball and establish a 'no throwing at faces' rule; use gentle underhand tosses.

title: Silent Comic Strip
materials: Printed comic strips with empty speech bubbles
desc: Students fill in empty speech bubbles of a comic strip to create a coherent story silently.
steps: Distribute a comic strip with empty speech bubbles to each student.
Set a timer for 10 minutes of absolute silence.
Students must write dialogue that makes sense narratively.
After time is up, students swap comics and read their partner's story.
variation: Cut the comic panels out separately and have students rearrange them before writing.
goal: Practice narrative dialogue, sequencing, and written register in a calm, focused environment.
example: 4-panel strip showing a character dropping groceries, meeting a stranger, laughing, and walking away—students invent the dialogue.

tips.lower_level: Provide a word bank of useful dialogue expressions ('Excuse me!', 'Oh no!', 'Let me help!') and allow simple 1-sentence bubbles.
tips.higher_level: Require specific grammar targets inside the dialogue (e.g., at least two idioms, a question tag, or past continuous).
tips.management: Remind students that 'silent' means zero talking during the 10-minute writing phase; play soft instrumental music.

title: Board Race
desc: Two teams relay race to the board to write words related to a topic.
steps: Divide class into two teams standing in lines.
Give the first student in each line a marker.
Shout a category (e.g., 'Animals').
Students run to the board, write one word, run back, and pass the marker.
The team with the most correct words after 2 minutes wins.
variation: Restrict words to a specific letter (e.g., Animals starting with 'B'). For ages 3-6, have them touch flashcards on the board instead of writing.
goal: Energize vocabulary recall, spelling accuracy, and team cooperation.
example: Category: 'Things in a Kitchen'. Team A writes: spoon, fridge, knife. Team B writes: stove, plate, fork.

tips.lower_level: Allow teams to whisper and help the writer spell from their line, or accept phonetic/nearly-correct spelling for half points.
tips.higher_level: Restrict answers to specific parts of speech (only adjectives or irregular past verbs) or require 6+ letter words.
tips.management: Tape a clear 'waiting line' on the floor 2 meters from the board so teammates don't crowd the writer.

title: Two Truths & A Lie
desc: Students spot the lie among three statements about their peers.
steps: Give students 3 minutes to write down two true facts and one lie about themselves.
In small groups, one student reads their three statements.
The group can ask 3 follow-up questions to try and catch them out.
The group votes on which statement is the lie.
variation: Teacher plays first to model the activity and build rapport.
goal: Develop question-asking skills, attentive listening, and natural personal storytelling.
example: Teacher model: '1. I have met a movie star. 2. I can juggle. 3. I hate chocolate.' (Students ask 'Which movie star?' to spot the lie.)

tips.lower_level: Limit statements to present simple ('I like...', 'I have...') and give question starters ('When did you...?', 'Why do you...?').
tips.higher_level: Ask students to craft subtle, believable lies using past experiences ('I used to...', 'I have never...') and defend them under cross-examination.
tips.management: Model all three statements and let the class grill you first—this sets the tone for believable lies and fun follow-up questions.

title: Vocab Pictionary
desc: Drawing vocabulary words for teammates to guess.
steps: Prepare a stack of cards with vocabulary words.
One student comes to the front, picks a card.
They have 60 seconds to draw the word on the board without speaking or writing letters.
Their team must guess the word.
variation: Use 'Claymation' style where they mold the word with playdough instead of drawing.
goal: Reinforce concrete vocabulary meaning and rapid mental association without native-language translation.
example: Word card: 'umbrella'. Student draws rainclouds + person holding a curved canopy; no letters or numbers allowed.

tips.lower_level: Let students draw from a visible unit word list so guessers have a narrowed pool of words.
tips.higher_level: Use abstract nouns, idioms, or compound phrases ('traffic jam', 'oversleep', 'jealousy').
tips.management: Enforce the 'No letters, no numbers, no speaking' rule strictly—one point penalty if the artist whispers a hint.

title: Sentence Surgery
desc: Physical rearrangement of jumbled sentence parts.
steps: Prepare envelopes containing strips of paper with words from a sentence.
Give an envelope to each pair of students.
Students dump the words and rearrange them physically to form a correct sentence.
They raise their hand when they think they have 'healed' the sentence.
variation: Include one 'distractor' word that doesn't belong in the sentence.
goal: Make English syntax, word order, and punctuation tangible through hands-on manipulation.
example: Cut strips: [Yesterday] [my sister] [carefully] [baked] [a giant chocolate cake] [for dinner.]

tips.lower_level: Color-code word cards by part of speech (nouns blue, verbs green, time expressions yellow) and use shorter 5–6 word sentences.
tips.higher_level: Use complex sentences with relative clauses, conditionals, or passive voice, and omit capital letters/punctuation.
tips.management: Paperclip or store each sentence in a numbered envelope so pieces don't mix between pairs and can be reused.

title: Back-to-Back Drawing
desc: Describing an image to a partner who cannot see it.
steps: Pairs sit in chairs back-to-back.
Student A is given a simple picture/diagram.
Student B has a blank paper and pencil.
Student A describes the image using shapes and prepositions (e.g., 'Draw a square in the center').
Compare the drawing with the original.
variation: Use Tangram puzzles instead of drawing for a tactile version.
goal: Sharpen precision with spatial prepositions, shapes, and active clarification questions.
example: Student A: 'Draw a medium circle in the top-left corner, and a triangle underneath it.' Student B: 'Touching the circle or separate?'

tips.lower_level: Pre-teach 6 key shapes and prepositions on the board (top, bottom, left, right, inside, next to) before pairs turn back-to-back.
tips.higher_level: Use complex scene diagrams or multi-step map routes instead of simple geometric shapes.
tips.management: Explicitly ban peeking until the timer ends; the big reveal and laughter at the end is the payoff!

title: Gallery Walk
desc: Peer review activity walking around the classroom.
steps: Post student work (essays, posters, etc.) on the classroom walls.
Give every student a pack of sticky notes.
Play calm music as students walk around 'viewing the gallery'.
Students leave one compliment and one question on a sticky note for each piece.
variation: Use different colored sticky notes for different types of feedback (e.g., Pink for praise, Green for growth).
goal: Encourage authentic reading, constructive peer feedback, and movement around the room.
example: Sticky note prompt: '★ Star: I loved how you described... | ? Question: What happened after...?'

tips.lower_level: Provide two sentence stems on the board for sticky notes: 'I like your ___.' and 'Good job on ___.'
tips.higher_level: Give each student a rubric checklist (e.g., thesis clarity, evidence, transitions) to guide their peer comments.
tips.management: Space posters evenly around all four walls so students don't bottleneck in one corner; play calm music to cue walking pace.

title: This or That
desc: Students choose between two options by moving to different sides of the room, explaining their choice.
steps: Ask students to stand in the middle of the room.
Present two related words or concepts (e.g., 'Apples or Bananas', or 'Summer or Winter').
Designate the left side of the room for option A and the right side for option B.
Students run to the side they prefer.
Ask random students to justify their choice in English.
variation: For older students, make the prompts moral dilemmas or debatable topics.
goal: Connect listening comprehension with movement and encourage every student to justify a preference.
example: Prompt: 'Summer vs. Winter' → Left wall = Summer, Right wall = Winter. Follow-up: 'Why did you choose Winter, Leo?'

tips.lower_level: Use concrete picture prompts (Pizza vs. Burger) and accept short reasons ('I like pizza because it is yummy').
tips.higher_level: Use nuanced dilemmas ('City life vs. Countryside', 'AI tutors vs. Human teachers') and require a 'whereas/however' comparison.
tips.management: Keep a clear center aisle free of backpacks before starting so movement between sides stays safe.

title: Devil's Advocate
desc: Students are forced to argue in favor of a statement they actually disagree with.
steps: Write a controversial statement on the board.
Ask students who agrees and who disagrees.
Pair up students and force them to argue the opposite of their actual belief.
Give them 5 minutes to prepare arguments.
Have pairs present their arguments to the class.
variation: Turn it into a formal mini-debate with a strict 1-minute timer for opening statements and rebuttals.
goal: Strengthen critical thinking, empathy for opposing viewpoints, and persuasive hedging language.
example: Statement: 'Social media should be banned for under-16s.' Frame: 'While some argue..., it is undeniable that...'

tips.lower_level: Brainstorm 2–3 arguments for both sides together as a whole class before pairing students up.
tips.higher_level: Run a quick 60-second rebuttal round where pairs respond directly to each other's counter-arguments.
tips.management: Frame the game clearly as roleplay ('Your job is to be a lawyer for this side') so students feel safe arguing unpopular stances.

title: Stop the Bus
desc: A fast-paced vocabulary game where teams race to fill categories starting with a specific letter.
steps: Divide the class into small teams.
Draw a table on the board with 5 categories (e.g., Animal, Food, Country, Verb, Color).
Call out a random letter of the alphabet.
Teams race to write one word for each category starting with that letter.
The first team to finish yells 'Stop the Bus!'.
Review the answers. If all are correct, they win the round.
variation: Make the categories grammar-focused, like 'Irregular Verb', 'Adjective', 'Preposition'.
goal: Activate broad vocabulary recall across multiple categories and encourage quick spelling checks.
example: Letter: 'M' | Animal: Monkey | Food: Mango | Country: Mexico | Verb: Make | Color: Magenta.

tips.lower_level: Reduce to 3 familiar categories (Animal, Food, Color) and allow 2 minutes per round before anyone can yell 'Stop the Bus!'.
tips.higher_level: Award 10 points for unique answers and 5 points for answers shared with another team, encouraging rarer vocabulary.
tips.management: Have teams put pens down immediately when 'Stop the Bus!' is called; verify spelling aloud on the board.

title: Kim's Game
desc: A classic memory game to test and reinforce new vocabulary items.
steps: Place 10-15 familiar vocabulary items on a tray.
Let the students study the tray in silence for 1 minute.
Cover the tray with a cloth.
Students must write down (or say aloud for ages 3-6) as many objects as they can remember.
Uncover the tray and count the correct answers.
variation: Instead of covering everything, secretly remove one item while their eyes are closed and ask 'What's missing?'
goal: Build visual memory and accurate recall of concrete nouns and classroom/unit vocabulary.
example: Tray items: eraser, key, spoon, coin, paperclip, apple, dice, watch, glasses, pencil.

tips.lower_level: Start with 6–8 items and review each item's name aloud together before starting the 1-minute silent study.
tips.higher_level: Require students to describe each item's position and appearance ('There was a blue pen next to a silver key').
tips.management: Use a large book or cloth to cover the tray cleanly; for big classes, walk the tray slowly down the aisles or project a photo.

title: Shout Out
desc: Students shout out known English words and then use them to make the longest sentence possible.
steps: Put students into groups and tell them to make a list of all the words they know in English.
Get the groups to write the words up on the board.
Have them use the mass of words to form the longest sentence possible.
variation: Limit words to a specific category to increase the challenge.
goal: Boost learner confidence by celebrating known vocabulary and practicing collaborative sentence building.
example: Board words: dog, happy, pizza, quickly, yesterday, park → 'Yesterday, the happy dog ate pizza quickly in the park!'

tips.lower_level: Provide a simple Subject + Verb + Object template on the board so beginners know how to connect their words.
tips.higher_level: Challenge teams to use every single word on their list in one grammatically accurate compound/complex sentence.
tips.management: Give each group a distinct board zone and color marker so words don't collide.

title: People Bingo
desc: Students mingle to find classmates matching specific descriptions on a bingo grid.
steps: Fill a bingo sheet grid with questions tailored to your students.
Give all students the bingo sheet.
Students mingle and ask each other questions to fill their blocks.
variation: Have students write the names in the boxes and shout 'Bingo!' when they get a full row or blackout.
goal: Promote authentic mingling, yes/no question formation, and classroom community building.
example: Grid square: 'Has a pet' → Student asks: 'Do you have a pet?' → Partner: 'Yes, I have a cat.' (Write partner's name).

tips.lower_level: Drill the exact question form for 3 sample squares aloud before letting students stand up.
tips.higher_level: Add a rule: you can only write each classmate's name once, and you must record one follow-up detail in the box.
tips.management: Play upbeat background music while students mingle; stop the music to signal everyone back to their seats.

title: Verbal Charades
desc: Students describe a word to the class without saying the word itself or using hand motions.
steps: Write nouns on slips of paper and put them in a hat.
Each student takes a slip and reads the word.
The student describes the word using only spoken English, without saying the word itself, and without using any physical gestures or descriptive noises.
Other students guess the word.
variation: Set a 30-second timer to make the game faster and more competitive.
goal: Practice circumlocution—explaining unknown or target words using synonyms, functions, and examples.
example: Target: 'refrigerator' → Clue: 'It is a big cold machine in your kitchen. You put milk and vegetables inside it.'

tips.lower_level: Write helpful starter prompts on the board: 'It is a kind of...', 'You use it to...', 'You find it in...'.
tips.higher_level: Include 2–3 forbidden 'taboo' helper words on each slip that the speaker cannot say.
tips.management: Keep speakers' hands behind their backs or holding a marker so they resist using charade gestures.

title: Dictionary Race
desc: The teacher reads dictionary definitions of words starting with a specific letter, and teams race to guess the word.
steps: Divide the class into 3 or 4 teams.
Choose a page from a monolingual dictionary and tell students the starting letter.
Read the definition of a word.
Students shout out the word they think is being defined.
variation: Have students take turns finding a word and reading the definition to the class instead of the teacher.
goal: Improve listening comprehension of formal definitions and strengthen dictionary/lexical awareness.
example: Letter 'B': 'A large container with a flat bottom and handle, used for carrying water or sand.' → 'Bucket!'

tips.lower_level: Paraphrase tricky dictionary words into simpler English on the fly and give a first-and-last-letter hint if stuck.
tips.higher_level: Read the exact dictionary entry including part of speech and multiple meanings; award bonus points for spelling.
tips.management: Use a buzz-in rule (raise hand + team name) instead of shouting over each other.

title: Hangman Expanded
desc: Classic hangman game with an added layer of providing descriptive clues about the word.
steps: Place the number of blanks for a word on the board.
Provide 2–3 descriptive clues about the word (e.g., for occupations: what they wear, where they work, what they do).
Students guess letters to reveal the word.
Discuss the meaning of the word once revealed.
variation: Use specific categories like occupations, locations, or animals for focused vocabulary review.
goal: Combine spelling deduction with active listening by anchoring letters to meaningful clues.
example: Blanks: _ _ _ _ _ _ _ (7 letters) | Clue 1: 'Works in a hospital' | Clue 2: 'Wears a white coat' → 'DOCTOR!' (wait, 6 letters) / 'SURGEON'.

tips.lower_level: Reveal the first letter and tell students the category before any guesses begin.
tips.higher_level: Let a winning student come up, choose a word from the unit glossary, and invent 3 clues for the class.
tips.management: Instead of a stick-figure gallows, draw a melting snowman or countdown rocket to keep the tone lighthearted.

title: Chain of Words
desc: A fast-paced chain where each new word must begin with the last letter of the previous word.
steps: The teacher starts by saying or reading a word.
Students join in by supplying a new word that begins with the last letter of the previous word.
Maintain a fast pace to keep energy high.
variation: Restrict the words to a specific category (e.g., 'Food' or 'Verbs') for a harder challenge, or have students throw a soft ball to choose the next speaker instead of going in a circle.
goal: Build rapid lexical retrieval and spelling awareness through letter-linked word chains.
example: Apple → Elephant → Tiger → Robot → Table → Egg...

tips.lower_level: Allow a 'lifeline' where a teammate can whisper a hint, and accept any valid English word.
tips.higher_level: Require words to be 5+ letters long or belong to one category (e.g., verbs only, or foods only).
tips.management: Use a 5-second clap rhythm or toss a soft ball to keep energy brisk without putting anxious learners on the spot.

title: Toilet Paper Ice-Breaker
desc: Students tear off sheets of toilet paper and must share one fact about themselves for each sheet they took.
steps: Pass around a roll of toilet paper and tell students to tear off some squares without explaining why.
Once everyone has their paper, explain the rules.
Every person must say as many sentences about themselves as the number of squares they have.
The teacher should introduce themselves first to show the example.
variation: Have other students formulate follow-up questions for every fact shared.
goal: Break the ice gently in a new group by turning a funny prop into structured personal introductions.
example: Student took 3 squares → '1. My name is Maya. 2. I love cooking pasta. 3. I have never seen snow.'

tips.lower_level: Write 4 safe topic prompts on the board (Name, Favorite food, Hobby, Family/Pet) so students aren't stuck for ideas.
tips.higher_level: Require at least one statement to be about a future goal or an unusual past experience.
tips.management: Cap the maximum squares at 5 or 6 (or say 'take what you need, up to 5') so one eager student doesn't have to give 20 facts!

title: Everyday Words
desc: Students guess everyday objects based on words or phrases typically printed on them.
steps: Write a phrase commonly found on an object on the board (e.g., 'CRUSH-PROOF PACK' or 'TWIST ON/OFF').
Have the class guess the object the phrase is written on (e.g., cigarette packet, jam jar).
Continue with other everyday phrases like 'BACK SPACE' or 'THANK YOU'.
variation: Have students bring in their own examples of everyday text to test the teacher and class.
goal: Build real-world environmental print awareness and deductive vocabulary reasoning.
example: Board text: 'BEST BEFORE / SHAKE WELL' → Juice carton! | 'CTRL + ALT + DEL' → Computer keyboard!

tips.lower_level: Show simple, high-frequency labels ('PULL / PUSH', 'OPEN / CLOSED', 'FRAGILE') with quick context hints.
tips.higher_level: Include idiomatic or technical labels ('DRY CLEAN ONLY', 'NO RE-ENTRY', 'USE BY') and discuss the difference.
tips.management: Award points per clue if you give 2–3 labels from the same object one by one.

title: Noughts and Crosses
desc: A tic-tac-toe game where teams must successfully answer a category-based question to claim a square.
steps: Draw a 3x3 grid on the board.
Assign a category to each of the 9 squares (e.g., Animals, Food, Sport, Countries).
Divide the class into Team O and Team X.
Teams choose a square and must provide a correct answer or sentence fitting the category to claim it.
variation: Do not allow repetition of any words previously used during the game.
goal: Gamify grammar or vocabulary review with strategic team decision-making.
example: 3x3 Grid: [Past Tense] [Food] [Prepositions] / [Irregular Verb] [Animals] [Adjectives] / [Opposites] [Jobs] [Pronunciation].

tips.lower_level: Put target vocabulary pictures or single words in each square; students just say the word or make a simple sentence.
tips.higher_level: Require a full, grammatically accurate sentence with 7+ words to claim the square; opposing team can challenge errors.
tips.management: Give teams 20 seconds to confer before answering so the game moves swiftly.

title: Act It Out
desc: Students write a short script based on a specific scenario and act it out for the class.
steps: Hand out plot scenarios to groups (e.g., 'A detective interviews witnesses to a bizarre noise').
Give groups 10 minutes to write a short script based on the prompt.
Have each group act out their scene for the rest of the class.
Encourage the use of target grammar, such as the past simple tense.
variation: Give them a scenario where they must resolve a conflict, like a neighbor complaining about a loud party.
goal: Integrate collaborative scriptwriting, target grammar in context, and expressive oral performance.
example: Scenario: 'Customer tries to return a broken robot at a shop.' Target: Past Simple + polite complaints.

tips.lower_level: Give a half-filled dialogue skeleton so groups only customize key lines and roles.
tips.higher_level: Add a surprise 'twist card' midway through rehearsal (e.g., 'Suddenly the power goes out!').
tips.management: Give shy students non-speaking or narrator/sound-effects roles if they prefer, while keeping scriptwriting collaborative.

title: The Balloon Debate
desc: Students take on the persona of a famous figure and debate why they should survive in a sinking hot air balloon.
steps: Assign or let students choose the identity of a famous historical or pop culture figure.
Set the scene: They are all in a hot air balloon that is losing altitude, and one person must be thrown out.
Each student must present a persuasive argument for why their character is too important to be thrown out.
The class votes on who is eliminated each round.
variation: Use professions instead of famous people (e.g., Doctor, Teacher, Artist, Engineer).
goal: Practice persuasive argumentation, roleplay empathy, and structured rebuttal speaking.
example: Characters: Doctor, Chef, Pilot, Musician, Scientist. Starter: 'If you throw me out, nobody will be able to...'

tips.lower_level: Let pairs co-represent one character and prepare 2 simple bullet points before speaking.
tips.higher_level: Hold a 30-second 'cross-fire' Q&A where other passengers challenge each speaker's usefulness.
tips.management: Keep votes lighthearted and award 'survivor' points; remind students to vote for the best *argument*, not their best friend.

title: Casino
desc: A grammar game where groups bet points on their ability to correctly identify and fix sentence errors.
steps: Hand out a list of sentences containing one or two errors.
Allot 100 points to each group.
Groups bet a number of points (maximum 10) that they can correct the error in a specific sentence.
Add points for correct answers and subtract points for incorrect ones.
variation: Allow teams to challenge another team's correction to steal their bet.
goal: Develop sharp proofreading, grammatical accuracy, and collaborative risk assessment.
example: Sentence: 'She don't like apples.' → Team bets $10 that it's wrong and corrects it to 'She doesn't like apples.'

tips.lower_level: Underline the general area of each sentence where an error might hide, and include clearly simple sentences.
tips.higher_level: Include subtle errors (collocations, articles, prepositions) alongside tricky *correct* sentences.
tips.management: Keep a visible scoreboard on the board so teams feel the casino excitement each round.

title: Puzzle Stories
desc: Students use yes/no questions to solve lateral thinking riddles.
steps: Read a short puzzle scenario to the class (e.g., 'A man walked into a bar and asked for water. The barman pointed a gun at him. The man said thank you and left.').
Students must ask yes/no questions to figure out the context.
Continue until they solve the puzzle (e.g., 'He had the hiccups').
variation: Have students bring in their own lateral thinking puzzles to test the teacher and classmates.
goal: Practice accurate Yes/No question formation and logical deductive reasoning.
example: Riddle: 'A man lives on the 10th floor. He takes the elevator down every morning, but only up to the 7th floor on rainy days?' (He's too short to reach button 10 without an umbrella!)

tips.lower_level: Write useful question stems on the board: 'Is he...?', 'Does she have...?', 'Was it...?', 'Did someone...?'.
tips.higher_level: Only answer strict Yes/No/Irrelevant—gently reject ungrammatical questions until rephrased accurately.
tips.management: Give one small hint after 10 questions if the class stalls so momentum stays positive.

title: Snowball Sentence
desc: Students reconstruct a sentence word by word, with each student repeating from the very beginning.
steps: Cut a story sentence into individual words and hand them out to students in the correct order.
Student 1 reads their word.
Student 2 reads Student 1's word, then their own.
Student 3 reads Student 1 and 2's words, then their own, and so on.
variation: Use this technique to practice days of the week or months of the year with lower levels, pointing at students randomly.
goal: Build auditory/working memory, natural rhythm, and sentence word-order awareness.
example: Sentence: 'The hungry brown cat quietly chased a tiny mouse.' (S1: The → S2: The hungry → S3: The hungry brown...)

tips.lower_level: Use a 6–7 word sentence with familiar nouns and verbs, and let students hold their word cards visibly at first.
tips.higher_level: Use a 12-word sentence with adverbs and prepositional phrases, then hide the cards for the final recite.
tips.management: Keep the pace upbeat and encourage supportive chanting rather than laughing at slips.

title: Repetitive Questions
desc: A rapid-fire drill where students must provide a unique answer to the same repetitive question.
steps: Ask a simple question to a student, such as 'What did you do yesterday?'.
The student answers quickly.
Immediately ask the next student the exact same question.
Each student must provide a completely new and unique answer without hesitating.
variation: Change the target grammar structure rapidly (e.g., shift from 'What did you...' to 'Where will you...').
goal: Build rapid automaticity with a target Q&A structure while discouraging memorized repetition.
example: Q: 'What are you going to do this weekend?' → A1: 'Visit my grandma.' → A2: 'Bake cookies.' → A3: 'Clean my room.'

tips.lower_level: Keep the question frame fixed for 1 full round and put a few picture prompts on the board for inspiration.
tips.higher_level: Require answers to include a reason ('...because...') or switch tenses every 5 students.
tips.management: Move unpredictably around the room (pointing or tossing a ball) so students stay alert and listen to avoid repeating.

title: Back to the Board
desc: A student faces away from the board and guesses a hidden word based on English clues from classmates.
steps: Have one student volunteer sit in a chair facing away from the whiteboard.
Write a word on the board (or stick a post-it note on their back).
The rest of the class gives clues in English without saying the target word.
The volunteer must guess the word.
variation: Put two students in chairs facing the class and make it a race to see who can guess their word first based on their team's clues.
goal: Strengthen descriptive speaking, synonyms, and active listening under team support.
example: Hidden word: 'astronaut'. Clues: 'This person goes to space in a rocket and walks on the moon.'

tips.lower_level: Allow the guesser up to 3 Yes/No questions ('Is it an animal?', 'Is it in this room?').
tips.higher_level: Ban gestures completely and require clues to use relative clauses ('It's a person who...', 'It's a place where...').
tips.management: Seat the guesser facing away from the board so they genuinely can't peek; rotate volunteers every word.

title: The Hot Seat
desc: One student sits facing the class. Their team must describe a hidden word written on the board behind them.
steps: Divide the class into two teams.
Place a chair at the front facing the class (the 'Hot Seat').
A volunteer from Team A sits in the chair.
Write a target vocabulary word on the board directly behind the student.
Team A has 60 seconds to describe the word to their teammate without using the word itself, spelling it, or translating it.
If the student guesses correctly, they get a point. Swap teams and repeat.
variation: For advanced students, allow the opposing team to make distracting noises, or use idioms instead of single vocabulary words.
goal: Encourage fast-paced team communication, paraphrasing, and vocabulary definition skills.
example: Board word: 'umbrella'. Team clues: 'You open it when it rains! It keeps your head dry!'

tips.lower_level: Display 5 unit words on the screen and secretly point to the active one, or allow 1 mimed clue.
tips.higher_level: Use phrasal verbs, idioms, or abstract nouns ('procrastinate', 'break the ice', 'deadline').
tips.management: Use a clear 60-second countdown timer and assign a student scorekeeper to keep rounds fair.

title: Find Someone Who
desc: Students mingle and ask yes/no questions to find classmates who match specific criteria on their worksheet.
steps: Distribute a 'Find Someone Who' grid to each student (e.g., 'Find someone who likes spicy food').
Students stand up and mingle around the classroom.
They must ask questions in English to find a match (e.g., 'Do you like spicy food?').
If a classmate answers 'Yes', the student writes their name in the grid box.
The first person to fill their entire sheet yells 'Finished!'.
variation: Require students to ask a follow-up 'Wh-' question (e.g., 'What is your favorite spicy food?') when they get a 'Yes' answer to extend the conversation.
goal: Get the whole class speaking simultaneously in authentic mini-interviews using target structures.
example: Box: 'Can play an instrument' → Q: 'Can you play an instrument?' → Follow-up: 'Which one?'

tips.lower_level: Use a smaller 3x3 grid with picture icons next to each prompt and pre-drill the question form.
tips.higher_level: Use Present Perfect ('Has been to another country') and require a past-simple follow-up note.
tips.management: Instruct students to hold pens and clipboards/notebooks and keep moving—never sit in groups filling each other's entire sheet.

title: Alphabet Race
desc: A fast-paced relay where teams race to write a word for every letter of the alphabet on the board.
steps: Divide the whiteboard into columns for each team.
Write the alphabet vertically down the side of each column.
Divide the class into teams and give one marker to the first student in each line.
On 'Go', the first student runs to the board, writes a word starting with any available letter, and runs back.
They pass the marker to the next student. The first team to complete the entire alphabet wins.
variation: Restrict the words to a specific lesson theme (e.g., only adjectives, or only things found in a kitchen) to increase the difficulty.
goal: Energize spelling and broad lexical recall across the entire A–Z alphabet.
example: A: Apple | B: Banana | C: Cat | D: Dog ... Teams fill letters in any order to finish first.

tips.lower_level: Use a shortened 10-letter list (A–J) or allow pairs to run up together with one word.
tips.higher_level: Skip easy letters or require every word to belong to one theme (e.g., Verbs, Countries, Adjectives).
tips.management: Give teams different colored markers and check for duplicate or illegible words before awarding the win.

title: Would You Rather
desc: Students are presented with two difficult choices and must select one, thoroughly explaining their reasoning.
steps: Write or project a 'Would you rather' dilemma on the board (e.g., 'Would you rather be able to fly or be invisible?').
Give students 1 minute of silence to think about their choice and formulate a reason.
Have students discuss and defend their answers in pairs.
Ask a few students to share their partner's answer and reasoning with the whole class to check listening comprehension.
variation: Have students write their own 'Would you rather' questions on scrap paper, put them in a hat, and draw them randomly for the class to discuss.
goal: Prompt thoughtful justification, conditional language ('I would rather...'), and respectful comparison.
example: Dilemma: 'Would you rather live without music or without movies?' Frame: 'I'd rather ___ because ___.'

tips.lower_level: Provide visual choices and a simple starter: 'I prefer ___ because ___.'
tips.higher_level: Require second conditional justification ('If I chose..., I wouldn't be able to...').
tips.management: Give 30–60 seconds of quiet thinking first so quieter students have an answer ready when pairing up.

title: Action Simon Says
desc: A classic listening game where students must only perform physical actions if preceded by the target phrase.
steps: Stand at the front of the class and give an imperative instruction (e.g., 'Simon says touch your nose').
Students must immediately perform the action.
Give an instruction without saying 'Simon says' first (e.g., 'Jump!').
Students must stay completely still. Anyone who performs the action is 'out' and must sit down.
The last student standing wins.
variation: Instead of eliminating students (which can cause disengagement), have 'out' students do three star jumps before rejoining the game.
goal: Train focused listening for imperatives and physical response (TPR) vocabulary.
example: Teacher: 'Simon says clap twice!' (Students clap) → Teacher: 'Touch your head!' (Students stay still).

tips.lower_level: Perform the actions yourself at first, then deliberately do the wrong action to test listening over watching.
tips.higher_level: Use multi-step commands ('Simon says touch your left elbow with your right hand and blink twice').
tips.management: Keep eliminated students active as 'judges' or let them do 3 jumping jacks to rejoin immediately.

title: Pictionary Relay
desc: A team-based drawing relay where students quickly sketch vocabulary words for their teammates to guess.
steps: Divide the class into two teams. Have them line up facing the whiteboard.
Show the first student in each line the same secret vocabulary word.
On 'Go', they run to the board and start drawing the word without speaking or writing letters.
The first team to correctly shout out the word gets a point.
The drawers go to the back of the line, and the next two students step up for a new word.
variation: For older teens, blindfold the person drawing and have a teammate guide their hand using only English directions (e.g., 'Up', 'Left', 'Draw a circle').
goal: Combine rapid vocabulary decoding with visual representation and lively team relay coordination.
example: Word: 'toothbrush'. Student draws a brush with bristles + smiley mouth; team shouts 'Toothbrush!' and runs next.

tips.lower_level: Give each team a printed mini-deck of picture/word cards so drawers don't misread the word.
tips.higher_level: Use two-word phrases or actions ('washing dishes', 'missed the bus', 'thunderstorm').
tips.management: Keep a damp cloth/eraser right by the board so the next drawer can wipe cleanly in 2 seconds.

title: Similarities
desc: Students ask each other questions to find three non-obvious things they have in common.
steps: Explain that students must find three things they have in common with a partner.
The similarities must not be obvious (e.g., they cannot use 'we both have black hair').
Model the activity by having the class interview you until they find three non-obvious similarities.
Have students mingle or work in pairs to find their similarities.
variation: For advanced classes, require them to find similarities based on abstract topics like fears, childhood memories, or future goals.
goal: Build rapport and authentic conversational questioning beyond surface-level small talk.
example: Not allowed: 'We both wear shoes.' Great similarity: 'We both dislike waking up early and have an older sister.'

tips.lower_level: Provide 5 question prompts on the board ('Do you like...?', 'Have you got...?', 'Can you...?').
tips.higher_level: Set a 3-minute timer to find 3 similarities with Partner A, then switch to Partner B to compare.
tips.management: Model one 'bad/obvious' similarity vs. one 'great/hidden' similarity with a student volunteer first.

title: The Diminishing Sentence
desc: Students build a long sentence together, then try to recite it as words are randomly erased one by one.
steps: Write a basic sentence on the board.
Have students add one word at a time to make the sentence as long and descriptive as possible.
Read the full sentence together.
Erase one random word from the board and have the class read the full sentence again, including the missing word.
Continue erasing words randomly until the board is almost blank, relying entirely on the students' memory to recite it.
variation: Start the next class with only the final word left on the board and see if the class can reconstruct the entire paragraph from memory.
goal: Reinforce sentence rhythm, chunking, and recall of grammatical function words.
example: Full: 'Yesterday, my tired dog slept quietly under the warm sofa.' → Gradually erase 'tired', 'under', 'quietly'...

tips.lower_level: Start with a 6–7 word sentence and leave the first letter of erased words as a scaffold.
tips.higher_level: Erase 2–3 words at a time or have pairs write the reconstructed sentence from memory at the end.
tips.management: Keep the whole class chanting together in rhythm—it makes memorization feel musical rather than stressful.

title: Reported Speech Chain
desc: Students introduce themselves and state a fact, and the next student must report it to the class before introducing themselves.
steps: Student A announces their name and a personal fact (e.g., 'My name is George and I like playing chess.').
Student B reports Student A's statement to the class using reported speech (e.g., 'She said she was X and that she liked X.').
Student B then introduces themselves and states a new fact.
Student C reports Student B's fact, then introduces themselves.
Continue the chain around the room.
variation: To increase the challenge, have the final student try to recount the reported speech for the last 5 students in a row.
goal: Practice accurate tense backshifting and pronoun changes in reported speech.
example: Alex: 'I love pizza.' → Sam: 'Alex said he loved pizza. My favorite animal is a fox.' → Maya: 'Sam said his favorite...'

tips.lower_level: Write the reporting frame on the board: '[Name] said (that) he/she [past verb]...' and keep facts in present simple.
tips.higher_level: Use varied tenses (can→could, will→would, went→had gone) and time expressions (today→that day).
tips.management: In classes over 16 students, run two parallel circles or groups of 8 so no one waits too long.

title: Grammar Treasure Hunt
desc: Students follow written clues hidden around the room or school to collect words that form a complete sentence.
steps: Write a 7-word sentence and write each word on a separate piece of paper.
Pin or hide the words in different locations around the classroom or school.
On each piece of paper, write instructions on how to find the next piece (e.g., 'Go upstairs, turn right and look beside the fourth door on the left.').
Give the first clue to the groups.
Once a group collects all the words, they must arrange them into the correct grammatical order to win.
variation: Instead of words forming a sentence, the hidden papers can be puzzle pieces or grammar questions they must answer before getting the next clue.
goal: Combine reading comprehension of directional clues with syntax problem-solving.
example: Clue 1: 'Look under the teacher's chair.' (Card word: 'ALWAYS') → Clue 2: 'Check beside the bookshelf.'

tips.lower_level: Use simple prepositions of place (under, on, next to) and keep all cards inside the classroom.
tips.higher_level: Write riddles or passive-voice clues ('This card is hidden where coats are hung').
tips.management: Color-code clue trails by team (Red Team only takes Red slips) so groups don't accidentally steal another team's clues.

title: Yes/No Taboo
desc: Students engage in conversation and try to trick their partner into saying the forbidden words 'Yes' or 'No'.
steps: Divide the class into pairs.
Explain that the words 'Yes' and 'No' (and their variations like 'Yeah' or 'Nope') are strictly taboo.
Students take turns asking each other rapid-fire questions designed to trick the other person into answering with a yes or no.
If a student says a taboo word, their partner gets a point.
Encourage students to elaborate and use full sentences to avoid the trap.
variation: Add 'Black' and 'White' to the list of taboo words to make answering descriptive questions much harder.
goal: Encourage extended conversational replies instead of one-word 'yes/no' answers.
example: Q: 'Do you like Mondays?' → Bad: 'No.' (Point lost!) → Good: 'Actually, I prefer Fridays because the weekend starts!'

tips.lower_level: Teach 3 safe alternative phrases first: 'Of course!', 'Not really!', 'Sometimes, when...'.
tips.higher_level: Forbid 'Yes', 'No', 'Maybe', and 'I don't know', forcing rich explanations.
tips.management: Run 60-second partner rounds, then rotate partners so students try new questioning traps.

title: Word Associations
desc: Students are given two unrelated words and must connect them through a chain of associated vocabulary.
steps: Write two completely unrelated words on the board (e.g., 'Bread' and 'Baby').
Put students into pairs.
Teams must write a chain of words that logically links the first word to the second.
For example: Bread -> Food -> Drink -> Milk -> Baby.
The pair that connects the words using the fewest possible steps wins the round.
variation: Play this out loud as a whole class circle game where each student says the first word that comes to mind based on the previous person's word.
goal: Expand semantic networks and encourage learners to explain logical connections between words.
example: Ocean → Fish → Dinner → Restaurant → Waiter → Tip → Money → Bank.

tips.lower_level: Choose two concrete everyday nouns ('Sun' and 'Ice cream') and allow 6–8 steps.
tips.higher_level: Challenge pairs to defend unusual connections aloud to the class ('How did you jump from Cloud to Keyboard?').
tips.management: Give a clear 2-minute countdown and compare the shortest valid chain on the board.

title: 3-Part Sentences
desc: Students draw random grammar constraints from boxes and must instantly form a correct sentence using a given verb.
steps: Label three boxes: 'Tense', 'Pronouns', and 'Positive/Negative'.
Fill each box with corresponding slips of paper.
Call a student to the front to draw one slip from each of the three boxes.
Shout out an infinitive verb (e.g., 'To Eat').
The student must immediately formulate a correct sentence using the verb and the three constraints.
variation: Have the rest of the class write down the correct sentence in their notebooks simultaneously to practice written grammar alongside the oral practice.
goal: Build grammatical agility across tenses, pronouns, and sentence polarity.
example: Drawn: [Past Simple] + [They] + [Negative] + Verb: 'go' → 'They didn't go to school yesterday.'

tips.lower_level: Limit boxes to Present Simple / Past Simple and Positive / Negative only.
tips.higher_level: Add a 4th box for 'Question / Conditional / Passive' or require a time expression.
tips.management: Let the student pick a classmate to be the 'grammar checker' before confirming the point.

title: Name As Many
desc: Students compete to name as many items as possible within a specific, challenging category.
steps: Divide the class into teams.
Read aloud or hand out a specific category card (e.g., 'Name 5 body parts above the neck with 3 letters' or 'Name the continents in alphabetical order').
Give students a set time limit (e.g., 60 seconds) to brainstorm and write down their answers.
The team with the most correct words wins the round.
variation: For lower levels, allow the use of dictionaries or expand the categories to be much broader.
goal: Activate focused brainstorming and precise lexical retrieval under tight constraints.
example: Card: 'Name 5 things that are round and smaller than a tennis ball' → coin, marble, grape, button, ring.

tips.lower_level: Use broad, familiar prompts ('Name 5 red fruits', 'Name 5 things in your backpack').
tips.higher_level: Use tricky constraints ('Name 5 irregular verbs whose past tense ends in -ought', 'Name 5 silent-letter words').
tips.management: Have teams write answers silently before sharing so teams don't copy each other's shouted ideas.

title: Word Explosion
desc: Students brainstorm and write as many English words as they can on the board to build confidence.
steps: Put students into small groups and have them list all the English words they can think of on a piece of paper.
Have groups send representatives to the board to write their words simultaneously.
The goal is to cover the entire board in a mass of English words.
Once the board is full, challenge groups to make the longest possible sentence using only the words on the board.
variation: Restrict the words to a specific grammatical category (e.g., only action verbs or only uncountable nouns).
goal: Warm up English recall effortlessly and turn scattered words into collaborative grammar.
example: Board explosion: cat, blue, run, school, happy, pizza, fast → 'The happy blue cat ran fast to school for pizza!'

tips.lower_level: Accept single words and simple 4-word sentences; praise the sheer volume of words they already know!
tips.higher_level: Award points only for sentences using at least 1 adjective, 1 adverb, and 1 conjunction from the board.
tips.management: Divide the whiteboard into team columns or hand out 4 markers at a time to avoid traffic jams.

title: Imagine a Photo
desc: Students mentally select significant personal photos and describe them to the class, prompting follow-up questions.
steps: Ask students to imagine they have brought 4 of their favorite personal photos to class.
Give them a few minutes to think about the people, places, or events in these imaginary photos.
Students take turns describing one of their photos in detail to the class or a partner.
The audience must ask follow-up questions to find out more information about the photo's context.
variation: Have the listening partner try to quickly sketch the photo on scrap paper based purely on the speaker's description.
goal: Develop vivid descriptive speaking and curiosity-driven follow-up questioning without needing real props.
example: Speaker: 'In this photo, I'm standing on a rainy beach holding a huge crab...' Partner: 'Who took the photo? Were you scared?'

tips.lower_level: Give 4 guiding questions on the board: Who? Where? When? Why is it special?
tips.higher_level: Require sensory details (colors, weather, sounds, feelings) and present continuous to describe the scene.
tips.management: Model one vivid 30-second imaginary photo description yourself before pairing students.

title: Blind Drawing: Places
desc: One student describes their home in meticulous detail while their partner attempts to draw an accurate floor plan.
steps: Divide the class into pairs: Student A (Speaker) and Student B (Drawer).
Student A imagines their house and must describe it in detail to Student B, as if describing it to a blind person.
Student B draws the floor plan or room exactly as described, remaining completely silent. Only Student A is permitted to speak.
Once finished, they compare the drawing to the speaker's actual house layout to see where communication broke down.
Swap roles and repeat.
variation: Have students describe a famous landmark, a fantasy castle, or their dream bedroom instead of their own home.
goal: Practice detailed spatial prepositions, room vocabulary, and active listening accuracy.
example: Speaker: 'When you enter the front door, there is a narrow hallway. On the left is a small bathroom...'

tips.lower_level: Limit the drawing to a single room (their bedroom) instead of a whole house.
tips.higher_level: Require precise comparative dimensions and prepositions ('opposite the...', 'in the far corner...').
tips.management: Seat partners back-to-back or hold a folder upright between them so the speaker doesn't gesture.

title: Jumbled Story
desc: Each student receives one sentence of a story and must mingle to put the narrative in the correct chronological order.
steps: Find a short, sequential story and cut it up so that each sentence is on a separate slip of paper.
Distribute one sentence to each student in the class.
Students must read their sentences out loud to each other and listen carefully to their classmates.
Without showing their papers, the class must physically arrange themselves in a line corresponding to the correct chronological order of the story.
Once they believe they are in order, they read the story aloud from start to finish to check.
variation: For smaller classes, give each student 2-3 sentences, or use the steps of a recipe instead of a narrative story.
goal: Develop discourse cohesion awareness (pronouns, connectors, time markers) through active mingling.
example: Slip A: 'First, Mia packed her suitcase.' Slip B: 'However, when she reached the airport...' (Students match pronouns & flow).

tips.lower_level: Use a 6-sentence story with clear time words (First, Next, Then, Finally) and number the first and last slips.
tips.higher_level: Remove obvious time markers so students rely on pronoun references ('it', 'they', 'the stranger') and cause-effect logic.
tips.management: Tell students 'Hold your paper against your chest—read aloud, don't show!' to maximize speaking and listening.

title: Body Parts Relay
desc: Teams race to correctly label the body parts of a designated 'mannequin' student using sticky labels.
steps: Write various body parts in large letters on separate pieces of paper and put tape on the back.
Divide the class into teams and have each team choose one student to be the 'mannequin' at the front.
Place a pile of body part labels at the back of the room for each team.
On 'Go', one student from each team runs to grab a label, runs to their mannequin, and sticks it on the correct body part.
The fastest team to correctly label all parts wins.
variation: Instead of a student mannequin, have them draw a giant monster on the board and label its bizarre body parts.
goal: Reinforce body vocabulary reading recognition through kinesthetic teamwork.
example: Labels: 'ELBOW', 'ANKLE', 'FOREHEAD', 'SHOULDER', 'WRIST', 'KNEE'.

tips.lower_level: Use 6–8 basic words (head, hand, foot, arm, leg, nose) and draw a simple cartoon outline on the board instead of tagging classmates.
tips.higher_level: Include trickier vocabulary (collarbone, wrist, calf, eyelash, knuckle, heel).
tips.management: Use gentle masking tape/sticky notes and remind students to place labels respectfully on arms/shoulders/paper.

title: Phrasal Verb Dicing
desc: Students roll dice to randomly combine verbs and particles, then must create a sentence using the resulting phrasal verb.
steps: Write a numbered list of 6 common verbs (1-6) and 6 particles (1-6) on the board.
Divide students into groups and give each group a die.
A student rolls the die twice: first for the verb, second for the particle.
The group must define the resulting phrasal verb and use it in a clear, unambiguous sentence.
If the combination doesn't exist, they roll again or invent a funny meaning for it.
variation: Have opposing teams challenge sentences they believe are grammatically incorrect to steal points.
goal: Demystify phrasal verb combinations and practice using them in clear, contextual sentences.
example: Verbs: 1.Get 2.Put 3.Look 4.Take 5.Turn 6.Give | Particles: 1.Up 2.Out 3.Off 4.On 5.After 6.Down → Roll 3+5 = 'Look after'.

tips.lower_level: Pre-select 6 verbs and 6 particles where most combinations are high-frequency ('turn on', 'put on', 'get up').
tips.higher_level: Require students to distinguish literal vs. idiomatic meanings or use the phrasal verb with a pronoun object ('put it off').
tips.management: If a rolled combo doesn't exist (e.g., 'give after'), allow a quick re-roll or award a creativity bonus for an invented definition.

title: Running Dictation
desc: A 'runner' memorizes chunks of a text pinned outside the room and dictates it to a 'secretary' who writes it down.
steps: Pin a few copies of a short text on the walls outside the classroom or at the far end of the room.
Divide students into groups and assign roles: one Runner and one Secretary (others can be Correctors).
The Runner runs to the text, memorizes as much as they can, and runs back to dictate it to the Secretary.
The Secretary writes exactly what the Runner says.
Clap your hands every few minutes to force them to switch roles until the text is fully copied.
variation: Include deliberate spelling mistakes in the pinned text that the Correctors must find and fix after the dictation is complete.
goal: Integrate reading, short-term memory, clear pronunciation, and accurate transcription in one energetic task.
example: Wall text: 4–6 sentences about a city trip. Runner reads 1 clause, runs back, dictates punctuation and spelling too!

tips.lower_level: Use 4 short, high-frequency sentences and let the runner go back as many times as needed.
tips.higher_level: Require exact punctuation, capitalization, and spelling; add a small penalty for each typo during final checking.
tips.management: Stress 'fast walking, no sprinting!' inside classrooms and tape texts far enough apart so groups don't crowd one wall.

title: Sentence Hangman
desc: A variation of Hangman where students guess entire sentences, focusing on syntax and grammar alongside spelling.
steps: Think of a full sentence and draw blank lines on the board for every letter, leaving spaces between words.
Divide the class into teams.
Teams take turns guessing either a single letter or an entire word that might fit the sentence's context.
If they guess a letter correctly, they get a point for every time it appears. If they guess a full word, they get points for all the letters in that word.
Encourage students to use grammatical clues (e.g., a three-letter word might be 'the' or 'and') to guess words before all letters are revealed.
variation: Use a sentence from a recent reading text or grammar lesson to reinforce current materials.
goal: Connect spelling, grammar collocations, and syntax prediction by guessing whole-sentence patterns.
example: Blanks: _ _ _ / _ _ _ / _ _ _ _ _ _ _ / _ _ _ _ _ _ ? ('Did you already finish?')

tips.lower_level: Give the first letter of the first word and tell students the sentence type (e.g., 'Past tense question').
tips.higher_level: Use complex sentences with conditionals or phrasal verbs, and penalize incorrect full-word guesses.
tips.management: Mark word boundaries clearly with slashes `/` or boxes so students can spot 1-letter and 3-letter grammatical clues.

title: Rhubarb!
desc: Students listen carefully as an opposing team reads a text out loud. If they hear a mistake, they shout 'Rhubarb!' to steal the reading turn.
steps: Divide the class in two and ensure everyone has the same piece of text.
One member of Team 1 starts reading the text out loud.
Team 2 listens intently. If the reader mispronounces a word or skips something, Team 2 shouts 'Rhubarb!'.
If the challenge is correct, Team 2 scores a point and takes over the reading.
If the challenge is incorrect, Team 1 scores a point and the next person in their team continues reading.
variation: Instead of a reading text, use a student reciting a memorized dialogue or irregular verb list.
goal: Promote attentive reading-along and sharp ear-training for pronunciation and skipped words.
example: Text: 'The train arrived late.' Reader says: 'The train arrive late.' → Opposing team shouts 'Rhubarb!' and steals.

tips.lower_level: Have the teacher read the text with 5 deliberate silly mistakes first so the class practices shouting 'Rhubarb!' together.
tips.higher_level: Students can challenge mispronounced word stress, dropped '-ed/-s' endings, or skipped punctuation pauses.
tips.management: Set a rule: if a team shouts 'Rhubarb!' falsely, they lose a point—this stops random shouting.

title: Desert Barter
desc: A survival roleplay where students must negotiate and barter their given items in English to become the richest survivor.
steps: Prepare slips of paper representing various survival items (e.g., '5 Litres of Water', '2 Camels', '10 Persian Carpets').
Assign point values to each item secretly based on a 'desert survival' scenario.
Hand out one slip to each student and tell them they must trade and barter to survive and become rich.
Students mingle and negotiate trades entirely in English.
At the end of the time limit, reveal the point values and have students calculate their wealth to find the winner.
variation: Act as a 'linguistic policeman' during the mingle; anyone caught speaking in their native language must sit out for one minute.
goal: Practice persuasive negotiation, numbers/offers, and spontaneous conversational English.
example: Useful phrases on board: 'What will you give me for...?', 'I'll trade 1 liter of water for 2 blankets.', 'Deal!'

tips.lower_level: Write 4 negotiation frames on the board and use simple concrete items (apple, flashlight, rope, bottle of water).
tips.higher_level: Add hidden 'condition cards' (e.g., 'Camel values double if you also own a blanket') to spark complex strategic deals.
tips.management: Use a clear 8-minute trading timer with a 1-minute warning before calculating survival points.

title: Up, Up, Up!
desc: The teacher reads a definition, and teams secretly write the word. On command, teams reveal their answers simultaneously.
steps: Divide the class into small groups and have each group appoint a secretary with a whiteboard.
Read out a definition of a target vocabulary word (e.g., 'This is a tool used for cutting wood').
Groups whisper to agree on the word, and the secretary writes it down secretly.
Shout 'Up, up, up!'. All secretaries must immediately raise their boards.
Award 10 points for the correct word, and deduct 5 points for spelling mistakes.
variation: Instead of definitions, read out a synonym, antonym, or translation to test different lexical relationships.
goal: Combine listening comprehension of definitions with collaborative team spelling accuracy.
example: Teacher: 'A person who designs buildings.' Teams whisper & write 'ARCHITECT' → 'Up, up, up!'

tips.lower_level: Give the starting letter or word length alongside the definition.
tips.higher_level: Read tricky near-homophones or commonly misspelled words ('accommodation', 'necessary', 'environment').
tips.management: Insist that boards stay flat on desks until 'Up, up, up!' so teams can't copy neighbors.

title: What Are You Doing?
desc: A fast-paced circle game where a student mimes one action but verbally claims to be doing a completely different action.
steps: Have the class stand in a circle.
Student A starts miming an action (e.g., brushing their teeth).
Student B turns to Student A and asks, 'What are you doing?'.
Student A must reply with an action entirely different from what they are miming (e.g., 'I am flying a kite').
Student B must immediately start miming 'flying a kite'. Student C then asks Student B, 'What are you doing?', and the chain continues.
variation: Speed up the game by eliminating students who hesitate for more than three seconds or who accidentally say the action they are actually miming.
goal: Drill present continuous speaking and listening comprehension while decoupling physical habits from speech.
example: Student A mimes swimming. Student B asks: 'What are you doing?' Student A says: 'I'm baking a cake!' → B mimes baking.

tips.lower_level: Put 10 illustrated action verbs on the board so students don't freeze trying to invent an action.
tips.higher_level: Add adverbs or specific objects ('I'm angrily ironing my neighbor's cat!').
tips.management: Keep the circle energetic; if someone freezes for 4 seconds, the whole class chants '3, 2, 1!' to help them pick an action.

title: Flashcard Telephone
desc: The teacher whispers a sequence of words to the back of the line. It is passed forward, and the front student must grab the matching flashcards.
steps: Place several flashcards on the whiteboard. Divide the class into two lines facing the board.
Go to the back of the lines and whisper a sequence of 3 or 4 flashcard words to the last students.
Those students whisper the sequence to the person in front of them, passing the message down the line.
When the message reaches the front, those students must jump up, grab the correct flashcards, and stick them on the board in the exact order heard.
Rotate the lines so a new student is at the front for the next round.
variation: Instead of flashcards, whisper a full sentence that the front student must quickly write on the whiteboard.
goal: Build keen listening discrimination and sequencing memory in an exciting team relay.
example: Whispered sequence: 'Apple, Elephant, Bicycle, Cloud' → Front student grabs those 4 cards in exact order.

tips.lower_level: Start with 2 flashcards and gradually build to 3–4 words; stand close enough to clearly model the first whisper.
tips.higher_level: Whisper a short 5-word sentence or preposition instruction ('Put the cat under the chair').
tips.management: Require whispers—anyone shouting aloud loses the round for their team.

title: Just Do It! (Mime, Speak, Draw)
materials: Vocabulary cards labeled M, S, or D
desc: Students draw a card and must convey the vocabulary word to their team by either Miming, Speaking, or Drawing, as dictated by the card.
steps: Create vocabulary cards and write M (Mime), S (Speak), or D (Draw) next to each word.
Divide the class into teams.
One student from a team comes up, looks at a card, and returns to their team.
They must instantly Mime, Speak (describe without saying the word), or Draw the word to get their team to guess it.
Keep a strict time limit (e.g., 45 seconds) for each round.
variation: Award bonus points if the guessing team can also provide the correct preposition or spell the word correctly once guessed.
goal: Vary vocabulary retrieval across kinesthetic (Mime), verbal (Speak), and visual (Draw) modes.
example: Card: 'SNEAKY [M]' → Mime tiptoeing quietly! | Card: 'VOLCANO [S]' → Describe without saying lava/mountain!

tips.lower_level: Let the team see the list of 12 unit words beforehand, or allow 60 seconds per card.
tips.higher_level: Include abstract concepts and award double points if the guesser uses the word accurately in a sentence.
tips.management: Make sure you have a clear signal for switching teams and track scores visibly.

title: Coffeepot
desc: The teacher replaces a mystery verb with the nonsense word 'coffeepot'. Students ask yes/no questions using the word to guess the real verb.
steps: Secretly choose an action verb (e.g., 'to swim').
Give the class a few example sentences replacing the verb with 'coffeepot' (e.g., 'I like to coffeepot in the summer. I coffeepot in the water.').
Students must ask you yes/no questions using the word 'coffeepot' to narrow down the verb (e.g., 'Do you need special clothes to coffeepot?').
The student who correctly guesses the verb gets to choose the next mystery verb and run the activity.
variation: Use the word 'thingy' to replace nouns instead of verbs to practice asking descriptive questions about objects.
goal: Practice verb-based Yes/No questions, collocations, and logical deduction.
example: Mystery verb: 'sleep'. Clues: 'Everyone coffeepots at night. You need a bed to coffeepot well.'

tips.lower_level: Provide 4 sample questions on the board: 'Do you coffeepot at school?', 'Can animals coffeepot?', 'Is it noisy?'.
tips.higher_level: Ban direct guesses until at least 5 deductive questions have been asked; include irregular/phrasal verbs.
tips.management: Remind students to conjugate 'coffeepot' properly ('Did you coffeepot yesterday?', 'Are you coffeepotting?').

title: Words from Words
desc: Students are given one long target word and must extract and create as many smaller, independent words from its letters as possible.
steps: Write a long, letter-rich word on the board (e.g., 'INTERNATIONAL' or 'DICTIONARY').
Put students in pairs and give them exactly 3 minutes to find as many smaller words hidden inside the main word as possible.
Letters can only be used as many times as they appear in the original word.
The pair with the most correctly spelled English words at the end of the time limit wins.
variation: Add a rule that words must be at least three letters long, or award double points for words related to the current lesson's theme.
goal: Strengthen English spelling patterns, vowel-consonant combinations, and vocabulary recall.
example: Base word: 'CELEBRATION' → cat, rat, rate, late, bear, train, clean, brain, table, reaction...

tips.lower_level: Allow 2-letter words (at, in, on, to) and let pairs use dictionaries to verify spelling.
tips.higher_level: Only count 4+ letter words; award 3 bonus points for any 6+ letter word found.
tips.management: Write the base word in huge block letters at the top of the board and run a visible 3-minute countdown.

title: Fortunately Unfortunately Story
desc: Students collaboratively create a story alternating between positive and negative events.
steps: Teacher starts a story with a sentence.
Next student adds a sentence starting with 'Fortunately...'.
Next student continues with 'Unfortunately...'.
Continue around the class.
variation: Students must use a specific grammar structure.
goal: Encourage spontaneous storytelling, contrast connectors ('Fortunately/Unfortunately'), and creative listening.
example: T: 'Max won a free ticket to Paris.' S1: 'Unfortunately, he missed the plane.' S2: 'Fortunately, he met a pilot...'

tips.lower_level: Keep sentences short (Past Simple) and write 'Fortunately (Good!)' and 'Unfortunately (Bad!)' on the board.
tips.higher_level: Require cause-and-effect links to the previous sentence and ban abrupt resets ('Suddenly he died').
tips.management: Jump in playfully if the story goes off-track to steer it back with a funny plot twist.

title: Secret Words Story
desc: Students secretly choose words and hide them in a story while others try to guess them.
steps: Students secretly write three words.
They tell a short story including the words.
The class listens and tries to guess the secret words.
variation: Limit the story to one minute.
goal: Motivate attentive listening to peer stories while embedding target vocabulary naturally.
example: Secret words: 'banana, helicopter, nervous'. Story: 'When I saw the yellow fruit on the chopper seat, I felt uneasy...'

tips.lower_level: Display 10 candidate words on the board and tell listeners that 3 of them are hidden in the story.
tips.higher_level: Students must slip the words in seamlessly without pausing or over-emphasizing them; listeners get 1 guess per word.
tips.management: Give writers 3 minutes to jot bullet points before speaking so stories flow naturally.

title: Alphabet Chain
desc: Students build a chain of words following the alphabet.
steps: First student says a word beginning with A.
Next student says a word beginning with B.
Continue through the alphabet.
Students are eliminated if they cannot think of a word.
variation: Restrict words to a theme (animals, food, jobs).
goal: Quickly activate A–Z vocabulary recall and attentive listening across the class.
example: A: Ant → B: Bear → C: Camel → D: Dolphin... (Theme: Animals).

tips.lower_level: Allow students to pass once or get 1 teammate whisper for tricky letters like Q, X, Z.
tips.higher_level: Require every word to fit a single theme or part of speech (e.g., only adjectives or jobs).
tips.management: Skip or combine X/Z playfully, or keep a quick 5-second beat so the chain never drags.

title: TV Commercial Warmer
desc: Groups create and perform a short TV-style commercial that summarizes or persuades about a topic from the lesson.
steps: Give each group a reading/topic from the lesson or a prompt.
Ask groups to plan a 2–3 minute commercial that informs or persuades an intelligent but uninformed audience.
Allow 10–15 minutes to plan and rehearse.
Each group performs while others evaluate content and clarity.
variation: Record performances on a phone and review for pronunciation and clarity.
goal: Synthesize lesson content or persuasive language into a punchy, audience-ready mini-presentation.
example: Topic: 'Solar Energy' → 90-second commercial pitching 'SunBox 3000' with 3 persuasive benefits and a slogan.

tips.lower_level: Provide a 4-line script template: Hook, Problem, Product Feature, Catchy Slogan.
tips.higher_level: Require persuasive rhetorical devices (rhetorical question, rule of three, imperative call-to-action).
tips.management: Set a strict 10-minute prep timer and 2-minute performance cap so every group gets stage time.

title: Teach Pronunciation & Idioms for Hellos
desc: Turn a normal greeting moment into a mini-lesson on idiomatic greetings and connected pronunciation.
steps: During the greeting routine, note common greetings students use.
Explain cultural/pragmatic differences (e.g., 'How are you?' as a greeting).
Model reduced/casual pronunciation (e.g., 'Howzit') and practice with choral repetition.
variation: Collect regional greeting expressions from students and compare registers.
goal: Raise awareness of natural connected speech, register, and cultural pragmatics in everyday greetings.
example: Written: 'How is it going?' → Connected speech: 'Howzit goin'?' | Reply: 'Not bad, you?' vs. formal 'I am very well, thank you.'

tips.lower_level: Focus on 3 clear pairs: Formal ('Good morning, how are you?') vs. Friendly ('Hey! How's it going?').
tips.higher_level: Explore regional idioms ('What's the craic?', 'Long time no see', 'How have you been keeping?') and intonation.
tips.management: Use the first 5 minutes at the classroom door or final 5 minutes as a natural real-world wrap-up.

title: Classroom Signs & Pragmatics
desc: Use classroom wall signs to discuss implied meanings and pragmatic function of language.
steps: Point out real signs around the room (e.g., 'Please keep quiet', 'Thank you for not smoking').
Ask students to paraphrase the sign and explain the intended action.
Discuss subtle pragmatic differences between literal wording and intended meaning.
variation: Have students design an alternative sign using different pragmatic strategies.
goal: Help learners read between the lines of public signs—understanding politeness, warnings, and implied rules.
example: Sign: 'Thank you for not using your phone.' → Literal: Thanks. Implied pragmatic meaning: 'Put your phone away!'

tips.lower_level: Compare direct imperatives ('Don't run!') with polite signs ('Please walk').
tips.higher_level: Analyze ironic, legal, or culturally indirect public notices ('Trespassers will be prosecuted', 'Staff only').
tips.management: Snap 3–4 photos of local street/school signs beforehand or point to actual posters on your classroom walls.

title: Controlled Narrative Writing (Class-led)
desc: Teacher-led stepwise narrative building: class supplies adjectives, adverbs and details to build and then write a story.
steps: Teacher reads a base story and pauses for students to suggest adjectives and adverbs.
Write selected suggestions into the story and read it again.
Students pair-work to expand or complete a controlled worksheet version of the story.
Collect, peer-review or display finished stories.
variation: Turn into homework stages so students complete later stages independently.
goal: Scaffold narrative writing by co-constructing rich descriptive language together before independent drafting.
example: Base: 'A girl walked into a house.' → Class adds: 'A curious young girl crept quietly into an abandoned wooden house.'

tips.lower_level: Offer 2–3 adjective/adverb options per blank so beginners build confidence choosing fitting modifiers.
tips.higher_level: Have pairs continue the co-created opening into a suspenseful 2-paragraph climax using varied sentence openers.
tips.management: Keep the co-created story visible on the board while pairs write their worksheet version.

title: Paul's Birthday Party (Memory Chain)
desc: A classic memory chain where each student repeats all previous items then adds a new one (ideal for 'going to' and future forms).
steps: Teacher starts with 'I'm going to Paul's party and I'm bringing a... t-shirt.'
Next student repeats and adds another item.
Continue until a student forgets; then restart or vary with grammatical constraints.
variation: Restrict items to begin with a certain letter or be adjectives + nouns.
goal: Drill 'going to' + noun phrases while building focus and cumulative auditory memory.
example: T: 'I'm going to Paul's party and I'm bringing a cake.' S1: '...a cake and balloons.' S2: '...a cake, balloons, and juice.'

tips.lower_level: Cap the memory chain at 6–7 students per group so everyone succeeds, and mime each item as a memory cue.
tips.higher_level: Require alphabetical order (A-item, B-item, C-item) or adjective+noun pairs ('a giant purple umbrella').
tips.management: Use a 'no shame, team help' rule—if someone blanks, classmates can silently mime the forgotten item!

title: Grab Their Attention (Question Drill)
desc: A quick rapid-fire Q&A sequence from the teacher to get students focused and practicing basic questions.
steps: Write the lesson plan on the board.
Ask a rapid series of simple personal questions to random students.
If a student can't answer, ask a neighbour and then return to the original student.
After 15–20 quick items, begin the lesson.
variation: Focus the questions on lesson vocabulary or grammar forms.
goal: Snap the class into English-thinking mode immediately with rapid, personal Q&A.
example: T: 'Mia, what did you eat for breakfast?' → 'Sam, what color is Mia's bag?' → 'Leo, do you prefer mornings or nights?'

tips.lower_level: Keep questions concrete and high-frequency, smiling and nodding to encourage quick 2–3 word answers.
tips.higher_level: Throw in unexpected follow-ups ('Why?', 'Really? Since when?') to spark authentic micro-conversations.
tips.management: Keep the entire drill under 5 minutes—brisk pace is what grabs attention before diving into the main lesson.

title: What's in My Bag?
desc: Students ask yes/no and WH- questions to guess items in a bag; practices question forms and vocabulary.
steps: Teacher displays a closed bag and models sample questions.
Students ask yes/no or specific questions to narrow possibilities.
The teacher reveals item after correct guesses or at teacher's discretion.
variation: Students bring their own bag and swap roles.
goal: Practice forming Yes/No and Wh- questions naturally out of genuine curiosity.
example: Prompt starters on board: 'Is it made of...?', 'How big is it?', 'Do you use it every day?', 'What color is it?'

tips.lower_level: Put 5 real mystery items inside (e.g., spoon, sunglasses, key, apple, comb) and let students feel the bag from outside.
tips.higher_level: Limit the class to 10 total questions per object—they must strategize broad-to-narrow questions!
tips.management: Write the question frame on the board before starting so students ask full questions instead of shouting guesses.

title: Web Shape First Lesson Warmer
desc: Students form a 'web' by passing yarn—used to illustrate class community and cooperate.
steps: Students stand in a circle and pass the yarn in different orders to form a web.
Ask students to notice the shapes and discuss what the web represents.
Use the web as a metaphor for teamwork and class rules.
variation: Have students explain how they contribute to the 'web' in English.
goal: Create a memorable visual metaphor for classroom community, active listening, and mutual support.
example: Prompt when tossing yarn: 'Say your name, one thing you enjoy, and one way you can help our class succeed.'

tips.lower_level: Keep the spoken prompt simple: 'My name is ___, and I like ___!'
tips.higher_level: Once the web is formed, gently tug one strand or drop one side to discuss how everyone's participation affects the group.
tips.management: Hold onto the end of the yarn tightly when tossing the ball so the web forms cleanly without tangling.

title: Number Seven (Clap Game)
desc: Counting/clapping elimination game: students must clap for numbers containing or divisible by 7.
steps: Students stand in circle and count in turn, clapping instead of saying numbers that have 7 or are divisible by 7.
Mistakes lead to elimination or short penalty.
Last student standing wins.
variation: Change the taboo number to 3 or 5 for variation.
goal: Sharpen mental alertness, number fluency, and rhythmic focus at the start or middle of class.

tips.lower_level: Only clap on multiples of 5 or numbers ending in 0/5 first, and count slower.
tips.higher_level: Play with 7 AND 3 (clap for 7, snap for 3) or count backwards from 50!
