tips.management: Instead of sitting out permanently on a mistake, restart at 1 with a faster tempo or swap direction around the circle.

title: Have You Ever? (Experience Mix)
desc: Students write 'Have you ever...' questions, pass them, and others answer yes/no; great for past experience language.
steps: Students write a 'Have you ever...' question.
Fold and pass slips; receivers write Yes/No without reading the question.
Read outcomes aloud and discuss surprising items.
variation: Use as a mingle activity where students stand up to ask questions to classmates.
goal: Practice Present Perfect ('Have you ever...?') questions alongside surprising class bonding.
example: Slip Q: 'Have you ever eaten fried insects?' → Fold → Neighbor writes 'YES!' blindly → Read aloud: 'Leo has eaten fried insects!'

tips.lower_level: Give 4 starter prompts ('Have you ever been to...?', 'Have you ever seen...?', 'Have you ever lost...?').
tips.higher_level: After reading the funny mismatches aloud, ask the real owner and have them tell the true story if anyone actually said Yes.
tips.management: Collect slips in a hat and shuffle them well so nobody knows whose Yes/No landed on which question.

title: Guessing from Context
desc: Students deduce nonsense words' meanings from sentence context to practice inference skills.
steps: Teacher writes sentences containing nonsense words (e.g., 'Can you turn the zong on?').
Students discuss meaning using context clues and justify choices.
Reveal chosen meanings and discuss strategies used.
variation: Have students craft their own nonsense examples for classmates to solve.
goal: Teach students not to panic at unknown words by practicing context-clue reading strategies.
example: Board: 'It was pouring outside, so Maya grabbed her *blarg* before walking to school.' → Students deduce 'umbrella/raincoat'.

tips.lower_level: Use concrete nouns with obvious clues and ask 'Is it a noun, verb, or adjective first?'.
tips.higher_level: Use paragraphs with 2–3 nonsense words including verbs and abstract adjectives.
tips.management: Ask students to underline the *clue words* in the sentence that proved their guess.

title: Controlled Photo Stories
desc: Create a sequence of photos with captions to develop narrative and descriptive writing skills.
steps: Provide a series of photos or ask students to take/select their own.
Students arrange photos to tell a story and write captions or short sentences beneath each photo.
Combine into a booklet and share with the class.
variation: Use photo stories as prompts for roleplays or dialogues.
goal: Develop visual storytelling, sequencing connectors, and descriptive caption writing.
example: 4 photos: (1) Empty coffee cup, (2) Rainy street, (3) Lost key, (4) Smiling friend → Pairs sequence & caption with 'Meanwhile...'

tips.lower_level: Provide 3–4 pre-selected photos and sentence starters ('First...', 'Then...', 'Suddenly...', 'Finally...').
tips.higher_level: Challenge groups to tell the story from an unexpected point of view (e.g., the lost key's perspective).
tips.management: Print reusable laminated photo sets or display 4–6 numbered photos on the projector for groups to sequence.

title: Pass the Chalk (Speaking Floor)
desc: Teacher hands the chalk to a student who speaks on a topic for a few minutes, then passes the chalk to another student.
steps: Introduce a topic and pass the chalk to a student.
That student speaks for a few minutes, then passes the chalk to the next student.
Continue until several students have contributed.
variation: Use as a debate starter where passers must respond positively or negatively.
goal: Build student autonomy, active turn-taking, and confidence holding the speaking floor.
example: Topic: 'My ideal weekend'. Student speaks for 30–45 seconds, then passes the marker to someone who hasn't spoken yet.

tips.lower_level: Allow a 15-second minimum (2–3 sentences) and put 3 helpful bullet prompts on the board.
tips.higher_level: Require the next speaker to briefly react to the previous speaker ('Like Sam, I also... / Unlike Sam, I...').
tips.management: Use a soft plush toy or special 'speaking marker' and gently enforce 'only the holder speaks'.

title: Rewrite the Ending (Story / Movie)
desc: Students rewrite or re-imagine the ending of a movie/story to practice narrative language and creativity.
steps: Choose a familiar story or show a short clip.
Ask groups to create an alternative ending that changes one major plot choice.
Groups present and explain their endings, focusing on cause/effect language.
variation: Perform alternative endings as short skits.
goal: Practice cause-and-effect language, creative writing, and conditional ('What if...?') thinking.
example: Prompt: 'What if Cinderella never left her glass slipper behind?' Groups write & perform a 4-line new ending.

tips.lower_level: Choose a very short familiar fable (Tortoise & Hare) and let groups draw a 3-panel new ending with short captions.
tips.higher_level: Require third conditional reflection ('If the hero hadn't..., the villain would have...').
tips.management: Summarize the original ending in 3 quick sentences first so everyone starts on the same page.

title: Magic Wand Warmer
desc: Students discuss what they would change at work/school with a magic wand and justify the changes.
steps: Pose the scenario: 'You found a magic wand that lets you change three work-related things.'
Students discuss choices and reasons in pairs.
Share interesting changes and prompt follow-up questions.
variation: Change the target domain: home, school, government.
goal: Stimulate imaginative speaking and persuasive justification using 'would' conditionals.
example: Prompt: 'With 3 magic wand waves, what would you change about our school/city/workplace and why?'

tips.lower_level: Offer concrete sentence frames: 'First, I would change ___ because ___.'
tips.higher_level: Add a constraint: 1 change for yourself, 1 for your school/community, and 1 for the whole world.
tips.management: Hold up a ruler or marker as a playful 'magic wand' when calling on pairs to share their best idea.

title: Idioms Warmer (Head Cluster)
desc: Present several idioms linked by one key word; discuss meanings and create contexts.
steps: Write 3 idioms sharing a keyword (e.g., 'head') on the board.
Discuss literal vs. idiomatic meanings and provide example contexts.
Students compose short dialogues incorporating an idiom.
variation: Challenge students to invent new idioms and explain their use.
goal: Teach idioms in memorable lexical clusters rather than isolated lists.
example: Keyword 'HEAD': 'head over heels', 'keep your head', 'two heads are better than one', 'head in the clouds'.

tips.lower_level: Limit to 3 visual idioms and have pairs draw both the literal funny meaning and the real figurative meaning.
tips.higher_level: Compare clusters (e.g., 'HAND' vs. 'HEAD' idioms) and weave 2 idioms naturally into a 4-line dialogue.
tips.management: Always elicit the literal image first—students remember idioms far better when they picture the literal joke!

title: ESL Skiing (Paper Race)
desc: Teams race while using paper 'skis' to transport a team member; checkpoint tasks use lesson language.
steps: Divide the class into teams and give each team member two A4 sheets (their 'skis').
One student from each team (the 'skier') stands on two A4 sheets at the starting line.
Teammates move the sheets forward one at a time to create a continuous path.
The skier can only step onto a sheet that has been placed by a teammate, mimicking a ski glide.
Teams race to a task station, complete a specific language-based task, and race back to the starting line.
variation: Replace physical tasks with grammar questions for quieter classes.
goal: Blend kinesthetic teamwork with rapid checkpoint language review.
example: Station tasks: Fix 2 grammar sentences on a mini-whiteboard or match 4 vocab flashcards before skiing back.

tips.lower_level: Use carpet squares or laminated sheets if floors are slippery, and keep tasks simple (say 3 target words).
tips.higher_level: Make station tasks mini-puzzles (unscramble an idiom or correct a paragraph error).
tips.management: Safety first! Check floor traction beforehand and use slow, controlled stepping rather than sliding.

title: Cell Phone Guessing Game
desc: Teacher stages short one-sided phone conversations; students guess the caller and reason.
steps: Teacher pretends to take a short phone call and provides partial clues.
Students propose who the caller might be and why.
Add further clues until someone correctly identifies the caller and motive.
variation: Students script one side of a call for classmates to interpret.
goal: Train inferential listening by deducing context, relationship, and tone from one side of a conversation.
example: Teacher on phone: 'No, I specifically asked for no onions... Look, I've been waiting 45 minutes!' → Pizza delivery mix-up.

tips.lower_level: Use exaggerated tone and clear clues ('Yes, Doctor, my tooth really hurts!').
tips.higher_level: Play a subtle professional or emotional call where students deduce both relationship and subtext.
tips.management: Give pairs 30 seconds after your performance to agree on WHO, WHERE, and WHY before taking guesses.

title: Combine It! (Unusual Combinations)
desc: From a topic list, students create unusual item combinations and justify them using target vocabulary.
steps: Elicit a list of topic items (e.g., foods).
Pairs propose the most unusual combinations (e.g., chocolate + beef).
Each pair explains why it might work using descriptive language.
variation: Make it persuasive: pairs must sell their combination to the class.
goal: Spark lexical creativity, compound noun/adjective usage, and playful persuasive speaking.
example: Brainstormed list: umbrella, toaster, skateboard → Combo: 'The Umbrella-Skateboard' (stay dry while commuting fast!).

tips.lower_level: Use food combinations ('banana + pizza') and simple reasons ('It is sweet and salty!').
tips.higher_level: Pitch the strange invention to 'investors' in 45 seconds using persuasive features and pricing.
tips.management: Write 8–10 student-suggested items on the board first so pairs have a rich menu to combine.

title: Learn a Phrase (Gallery Learn)
desc: Students wander and pick up new idiomatic or collocational phrases from posted extracts and teach each other.
steps: Post extracts with interesting phrases around the room.
Students walk, study a phrase, and return to teach it to peers.
Practice usage with pair exercises.
variation: Give students a short quiz on phrases they learned at the end.
goal: Promote peer-teaching and active noticing of natural collocations and idioms in authentic texts.
example: Wall excerpt highlights: 'make up your mind' → Student reads context, returns to pair, teaches meaning + new example.

tips.lower_level: Highlight or bold the target phrase on each wall card and include a simple synonym hint at the bottom.
tips.higher_level: Don't highlight the phrase—students must pick a useful collocation from the paragraph themselves and justify why it's valuable.
tips.management: Run as a pair relay ('Runner' reads & teaches, 'Writer' records) to keep noise calm and purposeful.

title: Make Boring Grammar Personal
desc: Turn grammar practice into personalised interviews so learners practise forms in a meaningful way.
steps: After reviewing a grammatical form, set interviewing tasks (e.g., present simple: 'Do you drive to school?').
Students interview classmates using target tenses and report findings.
Highlight common errors and elicit corrections.
variation: Rotate forms each round (past simple, present perfect, etc.).
goal: Transform mechanical grammar forms into genuine personal communication.
example: Target: Present Perfect ('Have you ever...?') → Pairs write 3 real questions for each other and report 1 surprise.

tips.lower_level: Give 4 fill-in-the-blank interview questions ('Do you usually ___ on Sundays?').
tips.higher_level: Require 2 follow-up questions per answer to turn the drill into real conversation.
tips.management: Spot-check 2–3 pairs during mingling and put 2 common great sentences + 2 anonymous error corrections on the board afterward.

title: Passive Voice through TPR
desc: Use physical actions (TPR) to make passive voice meaning and form explicit (e.g., drop a book then form sentences).
steps: Perform an action (drop a book) and ask 'Who did it?'.
Elicit active sentence then ask about the object to elicit passive form.
Practice converting active sentences to passive in pairs using TPR examples.
variation: Use different tenses to practise passive voice across time frames.
goal: Make the meaning and focus-shift of the passive voice immediately visible through live physical actions.
example: Action: Teacher drops pen. Active: 'Mr. Lee dropped the pen.' Passive: 'The pen was dropped (by Mr. Lee)!'

tips.lower_level: Stick to simple concrete classroom actions (open door, tear paper, erase board) in Past Simple passive only.
tips.higher_level: Demonstrate actions in progress ('The paper is being torn') or hide who did it to show why passive omits the agent.
tips.management: Have a student close their eyes while another performs an action, forcing authentic passive questions ('What was moved?').

title: Impromptu Speeches (Keyword Draw)
desc: Students draw a key word card and give a 1–2 minute impromptu talk to practise fluency and organisation.
steps: Create a box of lesson-related keyword cards.
Each student draws a card and prepares for one minute.
Deliver a 1–2 minute impromptu speech; peers give brief feedback.
variation: Ask peers to summarise the speech in one sentence to check comprehension.
goal: Build public speaking confidence and rapid speech structuring (opening, point, example, closing).
example: Keyword: 'Coffee' → 60s prep: Hook ('Are you awake yet?') + 2 reasons + Quick sign-off.

tips.lower_level: Allow 30–45 second speeches in small groups of 4 instead of in front of the whole class.
tips.higher_level: Draw a second 'challenge card' (e.g., 'Include a rhetorical question' or 'Speak as a news anchor').
tips.management: Give all speakers a guaranteed round of applause and 1 positive peer note ('I liked your example about...').

title: Haiku Closer
desc: Compose a short haiku related to the lesson topic to reinforce imagery and concise language.
steps: Explain haiku structure (5-7-5 syllables) and give examples.
As a class, compose a haiku on the board modeling the process.
Students write their own haiku and share with a partner.
variation: Turn best haikus into a class display or voice recordings.
goal: Distill lesson vocabulary and core takeaways into crisp 5-7-5 syllable poetry.
example: Topic: Weather → 'Cold wind blows outside (5) / Raindrops tap on the window (7) / Warm tea in my hands (5)'.

tips.lower_level: Clap syllables together as a class on the board and provide a 5-7-5 template with boxes for each syllable.
tips.higher_level: Require at least 2 target vocabulary words from today's lesson inside the haiku.
tips.management: Model counting syllables on your fingers with the whole class before writing starts.

title: KWL Chart (Topic Primer)
desc: Use a K-W-L (Know / Want to know / Learned) chart to prime background knowledge before reading.
steps: Write K-W-L columns on the board.
Elicit what students already know (K) and what they want to know (W).
After reading, complete L (Learned) and compare to initial expectations.
variation: Use small-group K-W-Ls for larger classes and then report back.
goal: Activate prior knowledge, build student curiosity, and close the loop on learning gains.
example: Topic: 'Space Travel' | K: 'Mars is red' | W: 'How long does it take?' | L: 'Takes ~7 months!'

tips.lower_level: Let students draw a quick sketch or share 1 word in the K column if writing full sentences is slow.
tips.higher_level: Add a 4th column 'H' (How can we find out?) for unanswered questions in W.
tips.management: Leave the K and W columns up on the board during the lesson so returning to L at the end feels rewarding.

title: Optimist vs Pessimist Role Debate
desc: Pairs take opposite stances as optimist and pessimist on topical issues to practise perspective language.
steps: Explain 'optimist' and 'pessimist' and model with examples.
Assign roles and a topic to each pair.
Pairs discuss for 5–10 minutes, then switch roles for another topic.
variation: Hold a short class debate between optimist and pessimist teams.
goal: Explore modal/perspective language and contrasting viewpoints on everyday situations.
example: Topic: 'Rainy Monday' → Optimist: 'Great for plants and cozy tea!' Pessimist: 'My shoes are soaked and traffic is awful!'

tips.lower_level: Provide two starter bubbles on the board: 'The good thing is...' vs. 'The problem is...'.
tips.higher_level: Call 'SWITCH!' mid-conversation so students instantly flip from optimist to pessimist on the same topic.
tips.management: Keep topics relatable and funny (missed bus, pop quiz, broken phone) so both roles are lively.

title: Semantic Web (Vocabulary Map)
desc: Create a semantic web on the board for a central topic to activate and expand related vocabulary.
steps: Write target word in centre of the board.
Ask students to call out related words and branch them off.
Use branches to pre-teach vocabulary before reading or discussion.
variation: Make group webs and compare; the richest web wins.
goal: Organize scattered vocabulary visually into meaningful sub-categories and collocations.
example: Center: 'TRAVEL' → Branches: Transport (train, ferry), Packing (passport, luggage), Feelings (excited, jet-lagged).

tips.lower_level: Draw 3 main sub-branches for the class first (e.g., Places, People, Actions) so students know where to attach words.
tips.higher_level: Require collocation pairs on every branch (not just 'ticket', but 'book a ticket / boarding pass').
tips.management: Give groups large A3 sheets and colored markers, then post webs for a quick 2-minute gallery compare.

title: Peer Review Warm-up
desc: Students exchange written work and give reader-response (one praise, one suggestion) to build peer feedback skills.
steps: Students swap drafts with a partner.
Read and give one positive comment and one area for improvement.
Discuss feedback and decide on one revision to implement.
variation: Use colored sticky notes to distinguish praise vs. improvement.
goal: Develop constructive, specific peer-editing habits using a structured praise-and-grow framework.
example: Star ★: 'Your opening hook made me curious!' | Step →: 'Can you add one example in paragraph 2?'

tips.lower_level: Provide 3 specific checkboxes ('Capital letters?', 'Clear beginning & end?', '1 favorite sentence').
tips.higher_level: Assign each reader a specific lens (clarity, tone, evidence, or grammar precision).
tips.management: Remind students to give kind, actionable feedback ('Add a detail here') rather than vague notes ('Good' or 'Fix grammar').

title: Advice Letter to Future Students (Course Closer)
desc: At course end, students write short advice letters to future learners using modals and recommendation language.
steps: Explain language for advice (should, ought to, if I were you).
Students write 2–3 paragraph letters giving practical tips to future students.
Share selected letters and display a compilation for the next cohort.
variation: Turn letters into podcasts or short videos.
goal: Consolidate modal verbs of advice while giving learners meaningful closure and pride in their progress.
example: Frame: 'Welcome to this class! You should definitely..., and if I were you, I wouldn't worry about...'

tips.lower_level: Use a structured postcard template with 3 prompts: 'My favorite lesson was...', 'You should...', 'Good luck!'.
tips.higher_level: Encourage authentic reflection on study habits, mistakes that helped them grow, and favorite class memories.
tips.management: Ask permission before keeping anonymous or signed letters to show next semester's incoming class—students love knowing real readers will see them!

title: Word Association Circle
desc: Students quickly respond with a related word to continue a chain of associations.
steps: Students stand or sit in a circle.
Teacher says a starting word.
The next student says a word related to it.
The chain continues around the circle.
Students who pause too long or repeat a word are out.
variation: Limit the associations to a specific topic such as food, animals, or travel.
goal: Warm up quick lexical retrieval and semantic connections in a lively, zero-prep circle.
example: Coffee → Morning → Alarm → Sleepy → Bed → Pillow → Dream...

tips.lower_level: Allow a gentle 5-second count and accept any logical link if the student can briefly explain why ('Coffee → Brown!').
tips.higher_level: Pause randomly and challenge a student to explain the last 3 links backwards.
tips.management: Avoid harsh elimination—if someone stalls, do a quick group clap and pass them the next starter word.

title: Back Drawing
desc: Students draw a picture on a partner's back which must then be reproduced.
steps: Students form lines or teams.
Teacher shows a picture to the last student in each line.
That student carefully 'draws' the picture on the back of the student in front using only their finger.
The drawing continues forward until the first student draws it on paper.
Compare the final drawing with the original.
variation: Instead of drawing, students describe the picture verbally.
goal: Channel kinesthetic energy into focused teamwork, spatial shapes, and descriptive communication.
example: Picture: A house with a sun and a tree (keep drawings to 3–4 bold simple shapes!).

tips.lower_level: Use single letters, numbers, or very simple shapes (triangle, star, smiley face) for younger learners.
tips.higher_level: Use a secret 3-letter or 4-letter vocabulary word written one letter at a time on the back.
tips.management: Respect personal boundaries—ask if everyone is comfortable with shoulder/back drawing, or offer drawing on a held mini-whiteboard/tabletop instead.

title: One Word Story
desc: Students collaboratively create a story by contributing one word at a time.
steps: Students sit in a circle.
Teacher begins with one word.
Each student adds one word to continue the story.
The class tries to keep the sentence grammatical.
Continue until a full story emerges.
variation: Students must include specific vocabulary chosen by the teacher.
goal: Sharpen active listening, parts-of-speech awareness, and collaborative grammar in real time.
example: S1: 'Yesterday' → S2: 'a' → S3: 'purple' → S4: 'elephant' → S5: 'danced' → S6: 'on' → S7: 'my' → S8: 'desk.'

tips.lower_level: Write a color key on the board (Noun / Verb / Adjective) and point if the story needs a verb next!
tips.higher_level: Include punctuation words ('period!', 'comma') and require at least 5 cohesive sentences.
tips.management: Go in predictable seating order so shy students can listen and prepare, and keep a quick steady beat.

title: The Categories Game
desc: Students list as many words as possible within a category starting with a chosen letter.
steps: Teacher writes a category on the board (e.g., animals).
Teacher also writes a starting letter.
Teams have one minute to write as many words as possible.
Teams share their answers.
Correct and unique answers score points.
variation: Students must use the words in a sentence to earn the point.
goal: Kickstart vocabulary brainstorming and team spelling with zero materials.
example: Category: 'Sports' | Letter: 'S' → Soccer, Swimming, Skiing, Surfing, Squash, Skating.

tips.lower_level: Pick high-frequency letters (B, C, M, P, S) and familiar categories (Food, Animals, Clothes).
tips.higher_level: Pick trickier letters (G, R, T) and award points *only* for unique answers no other team wrote.
tips.management: Set a crisp 60-second timer per round and play 3 rapid rounds with different letters.

title: Mystery Touch Box
materials: 5-6 familiar classroom objects or plastic toys
desc: Students reach inside a mystery box without peeking and use touch adjectives to guess the hidden object.
goal: Activate sensory adjectives (soft, hard, round, bumpy) and concrete nouns with high curiosity.
steps: Place 5–6 familiar items inside a cloth bag or covered shoebox before students see them.
Pre-teach 4 simple touch words on the board with gestures: soft, hard, round, long.
Invite one volunteer to put a hand inside without looking, feel one item, and describe it ('It is soft and small!').
The class guesses what it is ('Is it a teddy bear?') before the volunteer pulls it out dramatically.
example: Teacher prompt: 'Feel it! Is it hard or soft? Big or small?' Student: 'It is long and hard... I think it is a marker!'
variation: Put two items in at once and challenge older kids (7-12) to compare them ('This one is heavier than...').

tips.lower_level: Let the volunteer simply pick between two flashcards you hold up while they touch the hidden object.
tips.higher_level: Require full descriptive clues ('It's made of plastic and has a sharp point') before anyone may guess.
tips.management: Ensure objects have zero sharp edges and remind volunteers 'gentle hands, no peeking!'.

title: Phonics Hopscotch
materials: Floor cards or masking tape with letters/phonics sounds
desc: Students hop along a floor path of phonics cards, sounding out each phoneme or CVC word as they land.
goal: Connect kinesthetic movement with rapid phoneme-grapheme recognition and blending.
steps: Lay 8–10 large letter or phonics cards (e.g., sh, ch, th, ai, ee) in a stepping-stone path on the floor.
Model hopping down the path once while clearly saying each sound aloud.
Students line up in two teams and take turns hopping from stone to stone, calling out each sound.
At the final card, they say a word containing that sound (e.g., 'sh → sheep!') to earn a point and run back.
example: Path: [s] → [a] → [t] → blend 'sat!' | Or digraph path: [sh] → [ch] → [th] → [ee].
variation: Call out a target sound and have students hop *only* on squares that match that sound.

tips.lower_level: Teacher says the sound first and the student repeats it as they land on each square.
tips.higher_level: Use vowel teams or sight words and require the student to use the final word in a short phrase.
tips.management: Tape card corners securely to the floor so cards don't slip underfoot!

title: Freeze Dance Statues
desc: Students dance while music plays; when it stops, they freeze in a pose matching a called-out word, animal, or emotion.
goal: Burn restless energy constructively while reinforcing action verbs, animals, or feelings vocabulary.
steps: Clear a safe movement space in the center or beside desks.
Play upbeat music for 15–20 seconds while students wiggle or dance in place.
Pause the music suddenly and call out a target word (e.g., 'Frozen like an angry lion!' or 'Eating ice cream!').
Walk around admiring the 'statues' and ask 2–3 students 'What are you?' or 'How do you feel?' before resuming.
example: Music stops! Teacher: 'Freeze like a sleepy elephant!' (Students freeze with trunks drooping and eyes half shut.)
variation: Have students take turns being the 'Freeze DJ' who calls out the target emotion or animal.

tips.lower_level: Demonstrate each pose briefly the first time ('Show me happy! Show me monkey!') and avoid eliminating anyone.
tips.higher_level: Call out two-part prompts ('Freeze like a chef who dropped a hot pizza!') and have partners guess the story.
tips.management: Remind students to freeze in their own personal bubble without touching classmates.

title: Color & Shape Scavenger
desc: Students race safely to touch or point to something in the classroom matching a spoken color, shape, or texture.
goal: Anchor basic adjectives and classroom nouns to real objects in the learners' immediate environment.
steps: Review 4–6 colors and shapes around the classroom together.
Call out a prompt: 'Walk and touch something... BLUE!' (or 'something ROUND!').
Once students freeze touching an item, point to 3 students and ask 'What is it?' ('It's a blue book!').
Combine two attributes in later rounds ('Something green AND square!').
example: Teacher: '1, 2, 3... touch something YELLOW!' → Student: 'A yellow pencil!'
variation: Play 'Bring Me...' in small teams where one runner per team brings a safe matching item to the front.

tips.lower_level: Stick to single primary colors first and say 'Walk like robots' or 'Tiptoe' to control running speed.
tips.higher_level: Add prepositions and materials ('Touch something wooden under a desk').
tips.management: Enforce 'walking feet only' and remind students not to touch other people's personal bags or faces.

title: Puppet Echo Circle
materials: Hand puppet or class mascot plushie
desc: A friendly class puppet whispers or models target phrases in silly voices, helping shy young learners speak aloud.
goal: Lower speaking anxiety for early learners and drill target greetings, phonics, or short Q&A naturally.
steps: Sit in a circle and 'wake up' the class puppet together ('Wake up, Coco!').
Have the puppet greet the class and say a target phrase in a playful voice (whisper, giant voice, sleepy voice).
Students echo the phrase back to the puppet in the matching voice.
Walk the puppet around the circle so each child gets a friendly nose-boop or high-five while answering a 1-question prompt.
example: Puppet: 'Hello! My name is Coco. What's your favorite color?' Child: 'Blue!' Puppet: 'Ooh, I love blue too!'
variation: Have the puppet make silly mistakes ('Is this a banana?' while pointing at a shoe) so kids love correcting it ('No! It's a shoe!').

tips.lower_level: Accept single-word answers or simple pointing if a very shy child isn't ready to speak yet.
tips.higher_level: Let confident children hold the puppet and ask the circle question themselves.
tips.management: Keep the puppet 'special'—only bring it out during circle speaking time so kids stay captivated.

title: Sleeping Lions
desc: An instant calm-down game: students lie or rest heads down as 'sleeping lions' while listening quietly to soft vocabulary prompts.
goal: Transition an over-excited class back to calm focus while practicing receptive listening.
steps: Dim lights slightly or lower your voice to a calm whisper.
Students put heads on desks (or lie quietly on the rug) with eyes closed as 'sleeping lions'.
Walk slowly around the room whispering vocabulary words or target sentences.
Lions must stay completely still unless they hear a 'magic wake-up word' (e.g., today's target word 'apple!'), when they silently raise one hand.
example: Teacher whispers: 'Dog... chair... pencil... APPLE!' (Lions quietly raise one hand without talking.)
variation: Gently tap 2 calm lions on the shoulder to become 'hunters' who quietly watch for anyone wiggling.

tips.lower_level: Whisper single nouns and let kids stretch quietly like waking lions at the end.
tips.higher_level: Embed the magic word inside a calm mini-story so students must listen closely to full sentences.
tips.management: Use this immediately after a high-energy Stirrer before starting quiet desk work.

title: Flashcard Flyswatter
desc: Two team players race to swat the matching flashcard on the board when the teacher calls out the word or clue.
goal: Build instant word-to-image listening comprehension and reading recognition.
steps: Stick 8–12 flashcards low on the whiteboard within easy reach of students.
Divide the class into two lines and hand a clean flyswatter to the first student in each line.
Call out a vocabulary word (or a short clue like 'It says meow!').
The first student to swat the correct card earns a point and says the word aloud before passing the swatter.
example: Cards: cat, bus, apple, sun, book. Teacher: 'It's yellow and hot in the sky!' → Students race to swat 'sun'!
variation: Put written words instead of pictures on the board for early reading recognition.

tips.lower_level: Keep 6 distinct flashcards on the board and say the exact word clearly twice.
tips.higher_level: Give descriptive riddles, opposites ('Swat the opposite of cold!'), or spelling clues ('Starts with B!').
tips.management: Strict rule: swat the *board only*, never classmates—one swat per round so nobody hacks wildly.

title: Magic Hat Reveal
materials: 1 blank piece of card/envelope or hat
desc: Reveal a hidden flashcard millimeter by millimeter while students chant and predict what is inside.
goal: Spark excitement for introducing new vocabulary and practice prediction phrases ('Is it a...?').
steps: Hide a flashcard behind a blank piece of colored paper or inside a folder/hat.
Lead a fun class chant: 'Magic hat, magic hat, what's inside?!'
Slide the flashcard out very slowly, showing just a tiny corner of color or line.
Students raise hands and guess using 'Is it a ___?' until the whole picture is revealed.
example: Tiny orange tip appears → S1: 'Is it a carrot?' S2: 'Is it a tiger?' → Reveal full basketball!
variation: Flip the card upside down or sideways while revealing to make guessing trickier.

tips.lower_level: Accept single-word guesses and enthusiastically model 'Yes, it's a...! / No, try again!'.
tips.higher_level: Require justification ('I think it's a tiger because I can see orange stripes').
tips.management: Keep all students seated on the carpet/at desks so everyone has a clear view of the reveal.

title: Story Mat Sequencing
desc: Pairs arrange 4 illustrated story scenes in order on a mat and retell what happens using simple connectors.
goal: Practice chronological sequencing, story retelling, and basic time words (First, Then, Next, Finally).
steps: Read or act out a short 4-part story together first.
Give each pair or trio a shuffled set of 4 picture cards.
Pairs place the cards in order from left to right (1 → 2 → 3 → 4).
Walk around listening as partners point to each card and retell one sentence per picture.
example: 1: Boy plants seed. 2: He waters it. 3: Rain falls and sprout grows. 4: Big red flower blooms!
variation: Leave card #4 blank so pairs draw and explain their own surprise ending.

tips.lower_level: Number the spots 1–4 on a large paper mat and let kids retell with 2–3 key words per picture.
tips.higher_level: Require past tense verbs and connectors ('First he planted...', 'Finally it bloomed!').
tips.management: Store each 4-card set in a zip bag or envelope for instant reuse.

title: Pass the Stuffed Animal
desc: Children gently pass or roll a soft toy around the circle; whoever holds it shares their name and a quick favorite.
goal: Build a warm, safe circle routine for introductions and turn-taking with young learners.
steps: Sit with students in a circle and introduce a single sentence prompt ('My name is ___ and I like ___').
Hold the plush toy first to model clearly, then gently toss or roll it to a student.
The class claps or says 'Hi [Name]!' after the student speaks.
Continue until every student has held the toy and spoken once.
example: Model: 'My name is Ms. Lin and I like mangoes!' → Rolls toy to Leo → 'My name is Leo and I like dinosaurs!'
variation: Play music and pass the toy quickly; when the music stops, the holder answers a fun question.

tips.lower_level: Keep the prompt to just 'I'm [Name]!' or 'I like [Food]!' with picture flashcards in the center.
tips.higher_level: Challenge each student to remember the previous person's favorite before saying their own.
tips.management: Remind kids to say the receiver's name and make eye contact before gently tossing underhand.

title: Animal Sound Orchestra
desc: Divide the class into animal groups; the teacher acts as 'conductor' pointing to groups to speak, roar, or freeze.
goal: Practice animal names, volume adjectives (loud/quiet), and immediate response to visual cues.
steps: Assign 3–4 animal roles to different sections of the room (e.g., Lions, Ducks, Frogs, Snakes).
Stand at the front like a music conductor holding a marker as a baton.
Point at a group and raise your hand high (LOUD!) or crouch low (quiet!) as they say their animal name + sound.
Cross both arms in an X for instant total silence—praise the fastest quiet group!
example: Conductor points to Frogs + raises hands → 'FROG! Ribbit, ribbit!' → Crosses arms → Instant silence!
variation: Swap animal words for target phonics sounds (/s/, /b/, /m/) or classroom actions.

tips.lower_level: Show the animal flashcard while pointing at each section so kids connect word + sound.
tips.higher_level: Let a student volunteer be the conductor and give full English cues ('Ducks, quietly!').
tips.management: Practice the 'Crossed Arms = Instant Silence' signal twice before starting—kids love the game of stopping on a dime.

title: Listening Ears Clap
desc: Students put on imaginary 'listening ears' and clap once whenever they hear a secret target word or sound in your story.
goal: Focus young learners on active phonological or lexical listening during read-alouds or teacher talk.
steps: Announce one 'magic word' (e.g., 'red') or target sound (e.g., '/b/') and write/draw it on the board.
Tell students to cup their hands behind their ears ('Put on your listening ears!').
Read a short, expressive 6–8 sentence story containing the magic word 4–5 times.
Every time students hear the word, they give one crisp clap (or touch their nose).
example: Magic word: 'HAT'. Story: 'One sunny day, Sam put on his blue... HAT! [CLAP!] He walked to the park...'
variation: Assign two actions: clap for word A, tap knees for word B.

tips.lower_level: Pause slightly after saying the magic word the first time and give an exaggerated nod.
tips.higher_level: Use minimal pairs (e.g., clap for 'ship', stay still for 'sheep') to sharpen ear discrimination.
tips.management: Ask for 'one quiet clap' instead of wild clapping so nobody misses the next sentence.

title: Musical Chairs Vocab
desc: Students circle chairs while music plays; when it stops, the standing student names a flashcard to stay in or earn a bonus.
goal: Combine energetic movement with non-threatening individual vocabulary production.
steps: Arrange chairs in a circle facing outward (one fewer chair than students, or keep all chairs and mark 1 'Spotlight Chair').
Play upbeat music as students walk around the circle.
Stop the music! Everyone sits; the standing student (or Spotlight Chair student) picks a flashcard and says the word or a sentence.
Celebrate their answer with a class cheer and play another round without permanently knocking anyone out.
example: Music stops → Maya is on the Spotlight Chair → Picks 'banana' card → 'I like yellow bananas!' → Class cheers!
variation: Stick a flashcard under every chair; when music stops, everyone looks under their seat and tells their neighbor their word.

tips.lower_level: Keep all chairs (use 1 'Lucky Star' chair) so nobody sits out bored on the sidelines.
tips.higher_level: Require a full question or past-tense sentence using the drawn word.
tips.management: Insist on walking/marching in one direction—no diving or pushing for chairs.

title: Sticker Story Builder
desc: Students pick 3 picture stickers, stick them across a page (Beginning–Middle–End), and tell or write a 3-part mini-story.
goal: Give reluctant young writers an instant visual anchor for building a complete 3-sentence story.
steps: Fold a blank sheet of paper into 3 boxes labeled 1, 2, 3 (Beginning, Middle, End).
Let each student choose 3 random stickers (e.g., a frog, a bus, a cake).
Students stick one in each box and draw a quick background around each sticker.
Pairs share their 3-part story aloud (or write 1 simple sentence under each box).
example: 1. [Frog]: 'Once there was a green frog.' 2. [Bus]: 'He rode a big red bus.' 3. [Cake]: 'He ate chocolate cake!'
variation: Put 3 mystery stickers in an envelope so students have to invent a plot linking whatever surprise trio they get.

tips.lower_level: Keep it 100% oral drawing+telling for ages 3–6, writing down their dictated words underneath if helpful.
tips.higher_level: Require a problem in Box 2 and a solution in Box 3 using 'Suddenly' and 'Luckily'.
tips.management: Hand out exactly 3 stickers per student at the start so kids don't spend 10 minutes negotiating stickers.

title: Goodbye High-Five Chant
desc: Students line up at the door and give the teacher a high-five while saying today's 'exit password' phrase.
goal: End class on a warm, memorable personal connection while doing a 100% individual spoken check.
steps: Write or draw the 'Exit Password' on the board 2 minutes before dismissal (e.g., 'One new word you learned' or 'See you on Wednesday!').
Model the password and give a practice high-five in the air.
Stand at the classroom door as students line up.
Each child says the password clearly, gets a high-five (or fist bump/wave), and heads out smiling.
example: Password: 'Name one animal + bye!' → Student: 'Giraffe! Bye teacher!' → High-five!
variation: Offer a 'Menu of Greetings' taped to the doorframe (High-Five, Fist Bump, Silly Wave, Bow) for students to choose.

tips.lower_level: Hold up 2 flashcards at the door so the student just names whichever card you point to.
tips.higher_level: Ask a personalized 1-word recall question ('Tell me one past-tense verb!').
tips.management: Start packing bags 4 minutes early so the door high-five feels unhurried and joyful.

title: 3-2-1 Exit Ticket
desc: Students jot down 3 things they learned, 2 examples they can use, and 1 lingering question before leaving class.
goal: Check comprehension across every learner silently and gather instant feedback to plan the next lesson.
steps: Write '3 - 2 - 1' vertically on the board 5 minutes before the end of class.
3 = Three new words or ideas from today | 2 = Two example sentences | 1 = One question or confusing part.
Give students 3 silent minutes to write on a half-slip of paper or sticky note.
Collect tickets at the door as students exit and scan them to open your next class.
example: 3 words: recycle, landfill, solar. | 2 sentences: 'We should recycle plastic.' | 1 question: 'What is the difference between reuse and reduce?'
variation: Change to 3-2-1 spoken sharing with a partner if short on paper.

tips.lower_level: Shorten to '2-1': 2 new words (or drawings) + 1 favorite part of class.
tips.higher_level: Make the '1' a real-world connection ('One place I can use this outside class').
tips.management: Allow anonymous tickets if students feel shy admitting what confused them.

title: Snowball Reflection
desc: Students write one takeaway or anonymous question, crumple the paper into a 'snowball', toss it, and read someone else's aloud.
goal: Finish class with playful energy while surfacing honest questions and shared takeaways anonymously.
steps: Give every student a piece of scrap paper to write 1 thing they learned OR 1 question they still have (no names!).
Have everyone crumple their paper into a tight 'snowball'.
On '1, 2, 3, Toss!', everyone throws their snowball gently toward the center of the room.
Each student picks up a nearby snowball, opens it, and reads it aloud (or answers the question with a partner).
example: Opened snowball: 'I still don't know when to use FOR vs. SINCE.' → Teacher uses it for a quick 60-second clarification!
variation: Have students write an incomplete sentence from today's grammar on their snowball; the catcher must finish it!

tips.lower_level: Give a sentence frame: 'Today I learned how to ___.'
tips.higher_level: Have pairs answer the question on the snowball they caught before sharing 2–3 interesting ones with the class.
tips.management: Aim snowballs at the floor/center—never at faces—and recycle all paper in the bin on the way out.

title: One-Word Whip
desc: Rapid-fire round-the-room wrap-up where every student summarizes the lesson, mood, or key takeaway in exactly one word.
goal: Give 100% of students a fast final voice in under 3 minutes with zero setup.
steps: Ask everyone to think quietly for 20 seconds of ONE word that captures today's lesson or how they feel about it.
Explain that repeating a word is fine, or challenge them to pick a unique word.
Start at one corner and 'whip' around the room rapidly—one word per student, no interruptions.
Optional: Ask 2–3 students with intriguing words 'Why did you choose that word?'.
example: Prompt: 'One word for today's debate topic?' → 'Challenging!' → 'Eye-opening!' → 'Loud!' → 'Useful!'
variation: Turn it into a 'Six-Word Summary' whip for higher-level writing/reading classes.

tips.lower_level: Write 6 helpful adjectives on the board (fun, easy, hard, interesting, tired, proud) as optional prompts.
tips.higher_level: Ask for 'One noun or strong verb from today's text + a 3-word reason'.
tips.management: Keep the rhythm snapping briskly—never stop to lecture mid-whip so everyone finishes before the bell.

title: Two Stars & A Wish
desc: Students reflect on their own or a partner's work by naming two things that went well (Stars) and one goal for next time (Wish).
goal: Foster constructive self-assessment and growth-mindset reflection at the close of a project or lesson.
steps: Draw two stars (★★) and a shooting star/wand (☆) on the board.
Explain: 2 Stars = things you did well or understood today; 1 Wish = one thing you want to practice more next class.
Give students 2 minutes to jot or think of their 2 Stars & 1 Wish.
Have students share with a partner (or leave on a sticky note on their desk).
example: ★ I spoke English the whole group task. ★ I used 4 new travel words. ☆ I wish to practice past tense questions more.
variation: Use this as peer-feedback right after group presentations.

tips.lower_level: Let students draw 2 smiley stars and say 1 simple 'I can...' + 1 'Next time I want...' aloud.
tips.higher_level: Require specific evidence for each Star ('When we..., I successfully used...').
tips.management: Celebrate honest Wishes—remind students that naming a Wish is how learners level up fast.

title: Human Barometer
desc: Students stand along an imaginary confidence or agreement spectrum across the room to physically show where they stand.
goal: Gauge class mastery or final post-lesson opinions visually and spark brief closing justification.
steps: Designate one wall as '100% Confident / Strongly Agree' and the opposite wall as 'Need More Help / Strongly Disagree'.
Ask a closing prompt (e.g., 'How ready do you feel to use Conditionals?' or 'Did your opinion change after today's text?').
Students stand at the point on the line that matches their honest feeling.
Ask one person near each end and the middle to share why in one sentence.
example: Middle student: 'I understand the rule on paper, but I still hesitate when speaking quickly.'
variation: Have students compare where they stood at the start of the lesson (Warmer) vs. at the end (Closer).

tips.lower_level: Keep it simple with thumbs up / sideways / down at desks if space is tight.
tips.higher_level: Pair students standing at opposite ends for a 60-second debrief to help each other.
tips.management: Normalize standing toward the 'Need Help' side—thank students for honesty so you know what to review tomorrow.

title: Beat the Teacher Recap
desc: In a 2-minute lightning round, the class collaborates to answer review questions or tries to stump the teacher with lesson questions.
goal: Review the day's key vocabulary and grammar in a thrilling, cooperative whole-class finale.
steps: Draw a simple scoreboard: 'CLASS vs. TEACHER' and set a 2-minute timer.
Round 1 (60s): Rapid-fire ask the class 6 questions from today's lesson—any correct answer scores 1 point for Class; hesitating >5s scores for Teacher.
Round 2 (60s): Reverse roles! Students fire lesson-based questions to try to stump the Teacher!
Declare the winner with huge cheers before dismissal.
example: Teacher: 'Past tense of catch?' → Class: 'Caught!' (+1 Class). Student: 'Spell Tuesday backwards!' → Teacher sweats!
variation: Have teams prepare 2 'stump the teacher' questions in the final 3 minutes of group work.

tips.lower_level: Allow students to whisper-help each other during Round 1 so it stays collaborative.
tips.higher_level: Require students' stump questions to be grammatically accurate—if the question has a grammar error, Teacher wins the point!
tips.management: Playfully pretend to struggle on a student question every now and then—they love winning by 1 point!

title: Headline of the Day
desc: Pairs condense the main idea of today's lesson or reading into a punchy, memorable 6–8 word newspaper headline.
goal: Practice synthesis, concise wording, and headline register (omitting articles, strong verbs).
steps: Show 2 fun example headlines on the board (e.g., 'TEENS DEBATE AI: CREATIVITY WINS THE DAY').
Give pairs 3 minutes to distill today's entire lesson into one catchy 6–8 word headline.
Pairs write their headline in big letters (or shout them out).
Class votes by applause for the clearest or wittiest headline.
example: Grammar lesson on Passive Voice: 'MYSTERIOUS CULPRITS HIDDEN AS PASSIVE VOICE TAKES CENTER STAGE!'
variation: Add a 1-sentence 'sub-headline' explaining the most important rule or fact.

tips.lower_level: Remove the 8-word cap and provide 2 starter words ('TODAY WE... / CLASS DISCOVERS...').
tips.higher_level: Challenge pairs to use alliteration, a pun, or one vocabulary word from the lesson.
tips.management: Collect or snap a photo of the winning board headlines to display as a recap opener next class.

title: Muddiest Point Sticky Note
desc: Students stick a note on a door poster naming the single most confusing ('muddiest') concept from today's lesson.
goal: Surface hidden misconceptions early without embarrassing shy learners in front of peers.
steps: Draw a 2-zone poster or board section near the door: 'Crystal Clear 💎' and 'Still Muddy 🌧️'.
Hand out one sticky note per student 3 minutes before the bell.
Students write one specific thing they feel shaky on (or one thing that clicked!).
Everyone sticks their note on the way out so you can target tomorrow's warmer directly.
example: Muddy note: 'I still mix up affect vs. effect.' | Crystal Clear: 'Now I get how topic sentences work!'
variation: Digital/paperless version: have students hold up 1–5 fingers at chest height right before packing up.

tips.lower_level: Allow students to simply circle or copy a numbered board item (#1, #2, #3) that felt hardest.
tips.higher_level: Ask students to phrase their muddy point as a specific question rather than just a topic name.
tips.management: Always start the very next class by addressing the top 2 muddy notes—students feel genuinely heard.

title: Quiz-Quiz-Trade Exit
materials: Index cards or folded paper slips (1 per student)
desc: Each student writes 1 review question + answer on a card, mingles to quiz partners, swaps cards, and repeats.
goal: Maximize active retrieval practice across the whole class in the last few minutes of a unit.
steps: Give each student a card to write 1 quick review question from today's lesson on the front and the answer on the back.
Students stand up, raise a hand to find a partner, and quiz each other ('Tip–Tell–Praise' if stuck).
After both answer, they TRADE cards and move to find a new partner!
Collect cards at the door—bonus: you now have a student-made quiz deck for next week!
example: Front: 'Give 2 synonyms for happy.' Back: 'Joyful, delighted, thrilled.'
variation: Prepare the cards yourself beforehand for young learners using picture flashcards.

tips.lower_level: Write 3 question templates on the board ('How do you spell...?', 'What does ___ mean?', 'What's the opposite of...?').
tips.higher_level: Ban simple yes/no or single-word recall—require 'Explain why...' or 'Use ___ in a sentence'.
tips.management: Spot-check cards during the first 60 seconds so incorrect back-of-card answers don't circulate.

title: Head, Heart, Feet
desc: A holistic closing reflection: 1 idea for your Head (learned), 1 feeling for your Heart (valued), and 1 step for your Feet (action).
goal: Connect cognitive learning with emotional engagement and concrete next actions.
steps: Sketch a simple stick figure or 3 icons on the board: 🧠 Head (1 idea learned), ❤️ Heart (1 feeling/moment), 👣 Feet (1 next step).
Give students 3 quiet minutes to write one short line for each icon.
Pairs share one of their three reflections aloud.
Invite 2–3 volunteers to share their 'Feet' action step with the whole group.
example: Head: Learned 3 polite disagreement phrases. | Heart: Felt proud speaking up in my group! | Feet: Will use 'I see your point, however...' tonight.
variation: Turn into an oral quick-share in small groups of 3 when short on time.

tips.lower_level: Focus on just Head (1 word learned) and Heart (1 smiley/favorite game).
tips.higher_level: Use this at the end of a major unit or project to set authentic study goals.
tips.management: Share your own teacher Head-Heart-Feet reflection first—it builds immense warmth and trust.

title: Concentric Speed-Chat
desc: Students form an inner and outer circle facing each other; every 90 seconds the outer circle rotates one step for a fresh prompt.
goal: Give every student 5+ low-stakes speaking partners in 10 minutes while building class comfort.
steps: Arrange half the class in an inner circle facing outward, and the other half in an outer circle facing inward so everyone has 1 partner.
Display Prompt #1 on the board (e.g., 'What is your favorite meal and who makes it best?').
Start a 90-second timer—pairs chat nonstop.
Chime or clap! Outer circle steps one person clockwise; announce Prompt #2 and repeat 4–5 rounds.
example: Prompts: 1. Favorite weekend habit | 2. A movie you'd rewatch | 3. A skill you want to learn | 4. Morning bird or night owl?
variation: If desks can't move, run 'Speed-Chat Rows' where one side of each aisle shifts one seat forward.

tips.lower_level: Keep prompts concrete and provide follow-up questions on the board ('Why?', 'When?', 'With who?').
tips.higher_level: Reduce time to 60 seconds and ask students to summarize what the last partner told them at the end.
tips.management: If you have an odd number of students, join the circle yourself (or form one trio) so nobody waits out.

title: Four Corners Opinion
materials: 4 corner signs (Strongly Agree, Agree, Disagree, Strongly Disagree)
desc: Label the four corners of the room; read a statement and have students move to their stance corner and defend it.
goal: Warm up opinion language, polite disagreement, and whole-class movement.
steps: Post or point out the 4 corners: Strongly Agree, Agree, Disagree, Strongly Disagree.
Read a fun or thought-provoking statement aloud (e.g., 'Pineapple belongs on pizza' or '4-day school weeks are better').
Students walk to their matching corner and discuss *why* for 45 seconds with people in the same corner.
Call on 1 spokesperson per corner to explain; allow students to switch corners if persuaded!
example: Statement: 'Online classes are better than in-person classes.' Useful frame: 'We chose Disagree because...'
variation: Use 4 preference categories instead (e.g., Beach / Mountains / Big City / Countryside).

tips.lower_level: Stick to simple preference topics (Cats/Dogs/Birds/Fish) and accept short 'I like... because...' answers.
tips.higher_level: Require speakers to respond politely to another corner ('I understand Corner 1's point, however...').
tips.management: Remind students to decide independently—not just follow their closest friend's corner.

title: Line Up Without Speaking
desc: Students must organize themselves into a single ordered line (by birthday, alphabetical name, or wake-up time) using only gestures—then verify aloud!
goal: Spark instant laughter and teamwork, followed by structured spoken verification of dates, numbers, or time.
steps: Challenge the class to form one straight line in order of their birthday (January → December) with ZERO talking.
Start a 2-minute timer while students gesture, hold up fingers, and guide each other into place.
Once the line settles, go down the line from front to back having each person announce their birthday aloud in English!
Repeat quickly with a second prompt (e.g., alphabetical first name, or distance traveled to class—this time in English only!).
example: Verification round: 'My birthday is March 14th!' → 'Mine is March 29th!' (Cheers if they got it right!)
variation: Make Round 2 'Speaking Allowed, English Only' to practice comparative questions ('When do you wake up?', 'Earlier than me!').

tips.lower_level: Use simpler criteria like height or shoe color first, then birthdays using finger-counting for months.
tips.higher_level: Use trickier criteria like 'longest commute in minutes' or 'number of books read this year' in English-only mode.
tips.management: Ensure clear space along one wall so the line doesn't trip over backpacks.

title: Common Ground Venn
desc: Pairs or trios draw overlapping Venn circles to discover 3 surprising shared traits and 1 unique trait each.
goal: Encourage deeper personal conversation and practice 'Both of us...' vs. 'Whereas I...' comparison structures.
steps: Have pairs (or trios) draw two overlapping circles (a Venn diagram) on a blank sheet.
Challenge them to interview each other for 5 minutes to fill the overlapping middle with 3 *non-obvious* things they share.
In the outer circles, they each write 2 fun facts unique to themselves.
Pairs introduce their partner to a neighboring pair using 'Both of us...' and 'Only [Name]...'.
example: Overlap: 'Both hate cilantro, were born in October, and want to visit Japan.' Outer: 'Only Sam can solve a Rubik's cube.'
variation: Post the diagrams on the wall with names and have classmates guess which diagram belongs to which pair.

tips.lower_level: Write 5 conversation starters on the board (Food, Family, Hobbies, Travel, Fear/Dream).
tips.higher_level: Ban surface facts (school, city, age) and require comparative conjunctions ('Neither of us...', 'Unlike me, Maya...').
tips.management: Give a 2-minute halfway alert so groups don't spend all their time on just one topic.

title: Name & Motion Chain
desc: Each student says their name paired with an adjective or hobby and a signature gesture; the circle echoes and chains them together.
goal: Help teachers and classmates learn everyone's names rapidly on Day 1 using visual-kinesthetic memory.
steps: Stand in a circle. Model first: 'I'm Musical Maya!' (while strumming an air guitar).
The whole circle echoes back together: 'Hi Musical Maya!' (copying the air guitar).
The next student introduces themselves with a new adjective/hobby + action ('Dancing Dan!').
Challenge the circle every 4–5 people to recap all previous names and motions in unison!
example: S1: 'Sleepy Sam' (yawns) → S2: 'Soccer Sofia' (kicks) → Class: 'Sleepy Sam, Soccer Sofia!'
variation: For teens/adults, use alliteration ('Caffeinated Carlos', 'Curious Chloe') without requiring big silly motions if they prefer a fist-pump or wave.

tips.lower_level: Let young learners just say their name + 1 favorite animal motion instead of an adjective.
tips.higher_level: At the end, see if any volunteer can name the entire circle clockwise!
tips.management: In classes larger than 18, split into two circles so memory chains stay fun rather than exhausting.

title: Stand Up If...
desc: Students stand up whenever a spoken prompt applies to them, creating instant visual connections and quick follow-up chats.
goal: Break the ice effortlessly while reinforcing listening comprehension of varied tenses and habits.
steps: Start with everyone seated. Explain: 'If this is true for you, stand up!'
Call out increasingly fun prompts: 'Stand up if you drank coffee/tea this morning... if you have a younger sibling... if you've ever met a celebrity.'
Pause on interesting rounds to ask 1–2 standing students a quick follow-up question ('Who did you meet?!').
Invite confident students to call out the next 'Stand up if...' prompt.
example: Teacher: 'Stand up if you are wearing mismatched socks!' (Laughter, quick glance around, sit back down.)
variation: Play 'One Chair Short' musical version: everyone standing must swap seats across the circle!

tips.lower_level: Keep prompts concrete and visual ('Stand up if you are wearing blue!', 'if you like ice cream!').
tips.higher_level: Target specific grammar forms ('Stand up if you HAVE EVER...', 'Stand up if you WOULD LIKE TO...').
tips.management: Avoid sensitive personal prompts (money, grades, family structure); keep prompts lighthearted and inclusive.

title: Desert Island 3 Items
desc: Students pick 3 luxury/useful items to take to a desert island, justify their picks, and form a survival team with complementary items.
goal: Spark imaginative problem-solving, modal verbs ('We would need...'), and collaborative negotiation.
steps: Set the scenario: 'You are stranded on a tropical island with unlimited fresh water and fruit, and can bring just 3 extra items.'
Give individuals 2 minutes to write their 3 items and 1 reason for each.
Put students in groups of 4 to pitch their items and agree on the ultimate combined top 4 items for their island camp.
Groups present their 4-item survival plan and creative uses to the class.
example: Items: Fishing net, solar speaker, giant tarp, notebook. Pitch: 'With the tarp we can build shelter AND collect rain!'
variation: Ban practical survival tools (knife, lighter, phone) so students must justify hilarious luxury items.

tips.lower_level: Write 10 picture/word items on the board for students to choose 3 from.
tips.higher_level: Add an unexpected crisis ('A monsoon is coming!') halfway through group negotiations.
tips.management: Remind groups that every member must contribute at least 1 item or reason to the final pitch.

title: Postcard From Me
materials: Blank index cards or half-A4 sheets
desc: Students sketch a quick doodle-postcard representing their favorite place or hobby on the front and write a 3-line intro on the back.
goal: Give introverted and visual learners a low-pressure creative way to share who they are.
steps: Hand each student an index card. Front side: draw 3 quick doodles representing things you love (no words!).
Back side: write 3 short intro lines (Name, 1 dream/goal, 1 random fun fact).
Mingle in pairs: show ONLY the doodle front first so your partner guesses your 3 hobbies before flipping to read the back!
Swap cards and mingle with 2–3 partners, or pin postcards on a welcome board.
example: Front doodles: Headphones, mountain peak, ramen bowl → Partner guesses: 'You love hiking and spicy noodles?'
variation: Keep the postcards and return them on the final day of the course to see how students' goals progressed!

tips.lower_level: Provide 3 fill-in-the-blank lines on the board for the back of the card.
tips.higher_level: Challenge students to include one subtle 'mystery doodle' whose story takes 30 seconds to explain.
tips.management: Set a strict 4-minute drawing timer so perfectionists don't over-polish their sketches.

title: Mystery Picture Zoom
materials: Projector image or large picture covered with sticky notes
desc: Show an extreme close-up or covered picture and gradually reveal clues while students speculate using modals of deduction.
goal: Prime unit vocabulary and practice speculation language ('It could be...', 'It looks like...').
steps: Display a zoomed-in photo (or cover a printed poster with 6 numbered sticky notes).
Ask: 'What do you see? What could this be?' without confirming yet.
Peel off one sticky note (or zoom out slightly) after every 2–3 student predictions.
Once revealed, bridge straight into the day's lesson topic!
example: Sticky note #3 peeled → 'It looks shiny and round. Maybe it's a trumpet or a bicycle bell!'
variation: Let teams bet 1–3 confidence points on their guess after Sticky Note #2.

tips.lower_level: Model 'Maybe it's a...' and 'I see green/circles' with enthusiastic reactions.
tips.higher_level: Require modals of deduction ('It might be...', 'It can't be a... because...').
tips.management: If projecting, simply zoom a photo to 400% in your viewer and step out one zoom click per round.

title: Odd One Out Matrix
desc: Write 4 words on the board; pairs must argue why *each* of the four could be the odd one out using clever reasoning.
goal: Spark analytical vocabulary thinking, pronunciation/spelling noticing, and justification language.
steps: Write 4 related words in a 2x2 grid on the board (e.g., Banana, Apple, Carrot, Tomato).
Tell pairs: 'There is NO single right answer! Find a valid reason why ANY word could be the odd one out.'
Give pairs 90 seconds to invent as many clever justifications as possible.
Elicit reasons for all 4 words ('Carrot grows underground; Tomato is red AND a fruit; Banana is yellow and you peel it!').
example: Words: Run, Swim, Book, Jump → 'Book is a noun (or has a double letter); Swim happens in water!'
variation: Include pronunciation/syllable puzzles (e.g., tough, though, through, thought) for phonics/spelling warmups.

tips.lower_level: Ask for just 1 obvious odd-one-out first, then challenge them to defend a second choice.
tips.higher_level: Challenge groups to find a reason for *all four* words within 2 minutes—the most creative reason wins.
tips.management: Praise creative lateral reasons loudly—students realize there's no fear of being 'wrong'.

title: 60-Second Brain Dump
desc: Students silently write down everything they remember about yesterday's topic or a new unit theme in 60 seconds, then compare with a partner.
goal: Activate prior knowledge quickly and lower the barrier before introducing new reading or grammar.
steps: Write today's topic or yesterday's unit title in huge letters on the board.
Tell students: 'Pens ready! Write any words, phrases, or facts you already know—don't worry about perfection. 60 seconds, go!'
When the timer rings, pairs compare lists and 'steal' 2 new words from their partner.
Build a quick shared class list of top words on the board.
example: Topic: 'Space' → Student writes: planet, moon, astronaut, rocket, gravity, Mars, cold, telescope...
variation: Run a second 60-second brain dump at the end of class in a different pen color to visibly show growth!

tips.lower_level: Allow quick sketches alongside single words and celebrate whoever writes 5+ items.
tips.higher_level: Challenge students to group their brain-dumped words into Nouns / Verbs / Adjectives afterward.
tips.management: Stay completely silent with a visible timer during the 60 seconds—the urgency feels energizing.

title: Spot the Mistake Board
desc: Display 4 sentences on the board—3 contain realistic student errors and 1 is a tricky correct sentence; pairs hunt the errors.
goal: Turn common class mistakes into an engaging detective warmup without singling out any student.
steps: Before class (or quickly on the board), write 4 sentences based on recent lesson errors—make 3 flawed and 1 completely correct!
Tell pairs: 'Three sentences have a bug; one is 100% healthy. Find all 3 bugs and prove why #4 is fine.'
Give pairs 2–3 minutes to confer silently.
Invite volunteers to the board to fix the 3 bugs and explain the rule behind each.
example: 1. She can sings well. | 2. I am agree with you. | 3. He went to home. | 4. Have you ever been to Kyoto? (Correct!)
variation: Hide 2 spelling errors and 2 punctuation/grammar errors inside a short 4-line email.

tips.lower_level: Tell students which type of error is in each line (e.g., '1 spelling, 1 missing word, 1 verb ending').
tips.higher_level: Don't reveal how many sentences are correct—let pairs debate and defend every line!
tips.management: Always use anonymized or teacher-invented errors so nobody ever feels embarrassed.

title: Soundscape Guess
materials: Audio speaker + 20s ambient sound clip (cafe, train station, jungle, kitchen)
desc: Play a 20-second soundscape with eyes closed; students list everything they heard and infer the setting and story.
goal: Engage imagination and build descriptive Present Continuous / noun vocabulary before a listening or writing task.
steps: Ask students to close their eyes or rest heads down for 20 seconds.
Play an atmospheric sound effect clip (e.g., busy cafe: espresso machine, clinking cups, footsteps, rain).
Pairs list 4 things they heard and guess WHERE it is and WHO is there.
Play the clip once more while checking predictions and eliciting target words onto the board.
example: Sounds: Waves, seagulls, laughter, crunching footsteps → 'Someone is walking on a sunny beach eating snacks!'
variation: Have groups write the opening 3 lines of a mystery story set inside that soundscape.

tips.lower_level: Play distinct single sound effects (dog barking, ambulance, rain) and match to flashcards.
tips.higher_level: Use a complex layered audio scene and ask students to infer mood, time of day, and conflict.
tips.management: Cue up the audio clip tab before class starts so there is zero dead time.

title: Word Ladder Warmup
desc: Transform a starting 4-letter word into a target word by changing just ONE letter at each rung of the ladder.
goal: Sharpen phonics awareness, spelling flexibility, and strategic vocabulary search.
steps: Draw a 5-rung ladder on the board: Top word = COLD, Bottom word = WARM.
Explain the rule: change ONLY 1 letter per step, and every rung must be a real English word!
Demo the first rung together: COLD → CORD.
Give pairs 3 minutes to reach WARM (COLD → CORD → WORD → WORM → WARM) and challenge fast finishers to beat the step count.
example: CAT → COT → DOT → DOG! | HEAD → HEAL → HELL → TELL → TALL → TAIL!
variation: Provide a clue for each rung ('Rung 2: A thin rope' = CORD) to make it a structured phonics/vocab puzzle.

tips.lower_level: Use 3-letter CVC word ladders (CAT → DOG, HAT → PEN) so early readers succeed quickly.
tips.higher_level: Use 5-letter words or ban proper nouns and plural '-s' endings.
tips.management: Test your own ladder solution beforehand so you're 100% sure it's solvable!

title: Dictogloss Reconstruction
desc: Students listen twice to a short text read at natural speed—first pencils down, second noting keywords—then reconstruct the text collaboratively.
goal: Bridge listening comprehension and grammatical noticing by pushing learners to rebuild accurate syntax from meaning.
steps: Choose a compact 4–5 sentence paragraph rich in today's target grammar.
Reading 1: Pencils down! Read at natural speed while students listen purely for the big picture.
Reading 2: Read again at natural speed; students jot ONLY keywords (nouns, verbs, numbers—no full sentences!).
Pairs/trios spend 7 minutes pooling notes to reconstruct the original meaning as accurately as possible, then compare against the original on the board.
example: Text uses Past Perfect: 'By the time Mia reached the station, the last train had already left...'
variation: Focus comparison on 2–3 grammar features (articles, verb tenses, connectors) rather than word-for-word perfection.

tips.lower_level: Write 5–6 anchor keywords on the board beforehand and pause 2 seconds between sentences.
tips.higher_level: Use an authentic news snippet or dense academic paragraph with cohesive linkers.
tips.management: Remind students it's NOT a speed-dictation test—having slightly different wording with the same grammar and meaning is a win!

title: Jigsaw Reading Stations
materials: 1 text split into 4 short sections (A, B, C, D)
desc: Home groups split up to master one reading chunk in 'Expert Groups', then return to teach their piece so everyone solves a shared task.
goal: Turn silent individual reading into genuine purposeful speaking, summarizing, and peer-teaching.
steps: Put students in 'Home Groups' of 4 (numbered A, B, C, D).
All A's meet at Station A (and B's at B, etc.) as 'Expert Groups' to read their short section and agree on 3 key points.
After 6 minutes, students return to their Home Groups.
Each expert teaches their part orally (without handing over their paper!) so the group completes a 4-part summary or quiz.
example: Topic: 4 Inventors (A: Wright Brothers, B: Ada Lovelace, C: Marie Curie, D: Tim Berners-Lee) → Home group compares all 4!
variation: Post the 4 text chunks on walls around the room so Expert Groups stand and discuss together.

tips.lower_level: Provide 3 guiding comprehension questions on each Expert Sheet so weaker readers know what to extract.
tips.higher_level: Include a synthesis question at the end that requires combining clues from all 4 texts!
tips.management: Color-code the 4 sections (Pink A, Blue B, Green C, Orange D) for effortless grouping.

title: Socratic Fishbowl
desc: An inner circle discusses an open question while an outer circle observes actively and taps in to join the conversation.
goal: Elevate academic discussion quality, active listening, and evidence-based speaking in larger classes.
steps: Arrange 5–6 chairs in an inner circle ('The Fishbowl') plus 1 empty 'Hot Seat', surrounded by an outer ring of chairs.
Pose an open-ended question on the board and give everyone 2 minutes to jot 2 thoughts.
Inner circle discusses freely for 6 minutes using polite turn-taking; outer circle takes notes on strong arguments or evidence.
Outer observers can tap into the empty Hot Seat to add 1 point, or swap places halfway through.
example: Question: 'Should schools replace exams with portfolios?' Outer checklist: 'Tallied 1 follow-up question + 1 specific example.'
variation: Pair each inner speaker with 1 outer 'coach' who gives a 30-second halftime tip halfway through!

tips.lower_level: Put 4 discussion stems on the board ('I'd like to add...', 'Building on what ___ said...', 'Could you clarify...?').
tips.higher_level: Teacher stays completely silent during the fishbowl, letting students manage turn-taking and transitions.
tips.management: Giving the outer ring a concrete listening role (coach or tracker) keeps everyone 100% engaged.

title: Silent Chalk Talk
materials: 4 large poster papers or whiteboard zones
desc: Students circulate in total silence, writing responses to big prompt questions on posters and replying with arrows to peers' comments.
goal: Give thoughtful, quiet learners equal voice and create a rich written map of class ideas before speaking.
steps: Write 3–4 provocative questions or quotes in the center of large poster sheets around the room.
Give every student a marker and announce: 'For the next 8 minutes, NO speaking—only writing!'
Students walk around reading prompts, writing reactions, and drawing arrows to reply, agree (+), or question (?) peers' notes.
Break silence in small groups to summarize the top patterns on one poster for the class.
example: Poster prompt: 'What makes a city great to live in?' → Student A: 'Safe bike lanes!' → Student B draws arrow: 'Agreed! And reliable night trains.'
variation: Use different marker colors per round to track how ideas evolve.

tips.lower_level: Include visual pictures in the center of each poster and allow short 3–5 word phrases.
tips.higher_level: Require every student to post at least 1 original thought AND 2 direct arrow-replies to classmates.
tips.management: Play gentle ambient music if total silence feels awkward—it helps maintain the calm written focus.

title: Grammar Auction
materials: List of 8–10 sentences (some correct, some flawed)
desc: Teams inspect a sheet of sentences, then act as bidders in a live auction—buying sentences they believe are 100% grammatically correct!
goal: Make error analysis thrilling and incentivize careful collaborative grammar checking.
steps: Give teams 5 minutes to inspect 8–10 target sentences together and secretly mark which ones are 100% correct.
Give each team a $1,000 budget on the board.
Auction each sentence one by one ('Lot #1: She has lived here since 5 years. Opening bid $100—going once, twice, SOLD!').
After all lots are sold, reveal the answers: teams keep value ONLY for truly correct sentences (and earn a bonus if they can fix flawed lots!).
example: Lot #3: 'Despite the rain, we enjoyed the picnic.' (Correct! Worth $300!) | Lot #4: 'Everyone are ready.' (Flawed! $0 unless fixed.)
variation: Include 1 'Golden Sentence' worth double points if bought and defended.

tips.lower_level: Use 6 short sentences and highlight the target structure (e.g., 'Check the verb in every lot!').
tips.higher_level: Include subtle collocation, punctuation, and register traps alongside natural idiomatic sentences.
tips.management: Appoint one 'Banker' student to track team budgets on the board while you play the energetic auctioneer!

title: Carousel Brainstorm
desc: Groups rotate clockwise through poster stations every 2 minutes, adding fresh ideas and building on previous groups' lists.
goal: Generate massive collective brainstorming and categorize unit knowledge quickly through movement.
steps: Place 4–5 poster sheets around the room, each with a different sub-topic heading (e.g., Causes, Effects, Solutions, Vocabulary).
Assign each group a unique marker color and start each group at a different station.
Groups get 2 minutes to brainstorm and write ideas without repeating what's already on the sheet.
Call 'Rotate!'—groups move clockwise to the next station, read prior ideas, star the best one, and add 2+ new ideas until full circle.
example: Topic 'Healthy Living' → Stations: Food, Sleep, Exercise, Screen Habits, Mental Health.
variation: At the final home station, each group synthesizes the whole poster's colorful ideas into a 45-second summary.

tips.lower_level: Allow labelled drawings or single-word vocabulary items on the posters.
tips.higher_level: Require groups to add either 1 counter-argument or 1 real-world example to a previous group's note.
tips.management: Giving each group its own marker color creates instant accountability and makes rotation visually awesome.

title: Audio Detective
materials: Short 1–2 min audio dialogue or video played audio-only
desc: Play a short dialogue without video; students act as detectives across two listens—first solving Who/Where, then catching tone and hidden clues.
goal: Teach structured multi-listen strategies (gist → detail → attitude) rather than overwhelming students on Listen #1.
steps: Play a 45–90 second dialogue audio-only (hide any video screen).
Listen 1 (Big Picture): Pairs answer 3 detective questions: Who is speaking? Where are they? What's the problem?
Listen 2 (Fine Clues): Give 3 specific target details to catch (e.g., exact time, speaker mood, 1 key phrase).
Pairs compare evidence before revealing the video/transcript to check every clue!
example: Audio: Two friends arguing quietly at a train platform. Clue 1: Missed 4:15 express. Clue 2: Speaker B sounds relieved, not angry!
variation: Pause right before the final line and have pairs predict the ending before pressing play.

tips.lower_level: Put 3 multiple-choice settings on the board before Listen 1 so beginners focus their ears.
tips.higher_level: Ask detectives to identify sarcasm, hedging, or unspoken subtext in Listen 2.
tips.management: Always give pairs 30 seconds to compare notes *before* calling on anyone—it boosts listening confidence dramatically.
